data: We discover stores by component masks, then traverse bounded row ranges. Filter carries compile-time membership and access declarations; its include/exclude masks match physical stores. Excluded types constrain membership without supplying a component pointer. Read/write declarations also determine accessor permissions, invalidation, and device transfers.
data.exact-batch-membership#Exact batch membe:
EntitySelection retains triples of physical-store index, first row, and row count. Structural operations update those triples in place. A partial source range can move to a different store; the selection follows the affected rows and excludes preexisting destination rows. Kernel execution intersects that membership with the kernel’s filter.
Selections authorize their own mutations only when their guard is the sole active structural lock. Another query or selection prevents that mutation; nesting does not grant access through the other guard. Release, destruction, or context-manager exit releases the selection lock, including error exits.
Low-level HostStorage batch results use LockedEntityRange, rather than the system-level selection. Both retain bounded membership: extending a destination store must not make an older batch suddenly include unrelated rows. Sharing metadata avoids copying whole range lists when copying cursors; it does not share cursor position or authorize mutation.
data.from-membership-to-work#From membership:
A host context offsets its column pointers to the selected range’s first row and numbers local rows from zero. Threaded chunks repeat that rebasing. Device packing concatenates selected spans and scatters outputs to their original locations. Thus particle.idx is a context-local offset, never a stable handle or a full-world sequence number. See work mapping and transfers.
Implementation: Source, Source, Source. Evidence: test/world_entity_iterator_test.mojo, test/entity_selection_test.mojo, test/check_iteration_contracts.py; decision 0024 records the range contract.
data.guard-ownership-and-cursor-ownership#Gua:
query returns a read-only LockedEntityRange. The range owns a structural LockGuard and a cursor. Copies share immutable store-index/range metadata through ArcPointer, copy cursor positions independently, and acquire distinct lock bits. Exhaustion stops a cursor; it does not release its guard. Destroying one copy leaves the other copy’s guard intact.
The lock manager uses a fixed 256-bit lock set. Acquisition raises when those bits are exhausted; copying a guard aborts because Copyable cannot report an error. Moving transfers the existing bit. The guard only rejects structural changes that would invalidate borrowed rows. It provides no cross-thread exclusion or component-data synchronization.
Representation Ownership and purpose Entity Copyable stable identity; no lock or row borrow. Query row accessor Temporary read-only reference into a guarded store; cannot outlive its range. EntityRange Store index, first row, and row count; plain metadata owns no lock. LockedEntityRange Storage borrow and independent guard/cursor, including low-level batch membership. EntitySelection Movable, noncopyable exact membership plus one system-level structural guard. Kernel row accessor Invocation-local column pointers and row offset; no stable entity ID.

data:
The Scheduler owns a World and registered system values. Each scheduler phase visits systems in registration order: initialize once, update once per step, then finalize once. A system receives a SystemContext borrowing that world; its kernel receives only the columns, resources, and captures declared for that invocation.
The diagram separates ownership from temporary access.
Scroll horizontally to read the full figure.
Solid containment denotes ownership; arrows denote calls and borrowed access.
We retain host components in World.storage, resource sources in World.resources, and optional device allocations in the world. A spatial classifier is also an owned world value. KernelContext contains row count, column pointers, and binding descriptors; copying it does not copy the world or extend those allocations’ validity beyond the invocation. No context or row reference may escape its execution boundary.
data.caller-and-binding-lifetimes#Caller and:
A threaded run prepares contexts and bindings on the caller, retains an execution guard and structural guard, then joins every worker before releasing them. The world remains caller-confined: its active flag rejects reentrant execution, and copying, moving, or destroying an active world aborts. This flag is a lifecycle check, not a mutex for arbitrary external callers.
Resource bindings retain source leases and invocation-owned views. A device run retains native staging buffers until queued work completes, publishes outputs, then releases bindings. See bindings and transfers for failure behavior and structural guards for iteration ownership.
The thesis architecture predates SystemContext, device-copy ownership, and partition stores. Its mutable-World system signatures do not define today’s API. The adapted diagram describes roles and ownership, not object byte layout.
Implementation: Source, Source, Source. Evidence: test/scheduler_test.mojo, test/threaded_execution_test.mojo, test/resource_adapter_host_test.mojo.
data.one-system-multiple-kernel-invocations#O:
Move.update requests one run, but the executor chooses its invocation granularity. Sequential host execution calls the kernel for each nonempty matching physical range. Threaded execution can split ranges into chunks. Device execution packs ranges into one launch. Systems themselves remain ordered; threaded chunks do not make scheduler systems concurrent.
A side effect outside a kernel’s row loop therefore counts invocations, not simulation steps or entities. The work mapping explains how row offsets differ between those contexts. The checked particle types remain Position.x/y, Velocity.dx/dy, and Time.delta; the system is Move and its kernel is move in Your first simulation.

data: We store an owned SpatialClassifier and typed maintenance callback on the world. Its explicit read-only filter selects eligible compositions and classifier inputs. The current world holds one classifier. A UInt64 cluster key groups locality; neither key adjacency nor placement guarantees exact neighbors.
data.invalidations-before-movement#Invalidati:
The storage owns a queue of full ID/generation identities, sparse membership bits indexed by entity ID, committed keys, and a full-rebuild flag. Repeated input writes enqueue an identity once; classification reads its final values at the explicit boundary. Mutable input exposure and declared kernel writes mark conservatively, including device copy-back. Registration, structural changes, and explicit invalidation request a full rebuild.
The boundary separates callbacks from physical mutation.
Scroll horizontally to read the full figure.
All classifier callbacks finish before any row moves.
maintain_spatial first rejects a locked world. A clean call returns without row work. Otherwise it builds pending keys from the cache or a full scan, validates liveness/eligibility for dirty identities, and prepares permutations or partition placement. Classifier errors preserve prior order, committed keys, and pending invalidations. Once planning succeeds, typed movement repairs locations and commits keys, then clears dirty state. Allocation failure is fatal as in ordinary storage; this is not a general rollback transaction.
Mutable references cannot span maintenance. Low-level raw writes require explicit marking or invalidation because they bypass automatic tracking. System/kernel completion marks work but never runs spatial maintenance itself.
data.two-physical-layouts-one-logical-composi:
The adapted ordering/grouping figure shows the two implemented placement modes.
Scroll horizontally to read the full figure.
Partition stores share a component mask and logical transition node.
Default maintenance sorts affected stores by ascending key and applies typed permutations to IDs and every active column. Equal-key rows become contiguous; applications cannot depend on tie order. Clean rows can move when regrouping requires it.
Opt-in partition mode retains a canonical staging store for creation and structural transitions. Maintenance moves rows into one growable store per logical-archetype/key pair, swap-removes source rows, and repairs locations. Destination growth can relocate existing values. Empty cluster stores release row allocations and recycle directory slots with fresh incarnations. Nonempty stores retain spare capacity; there is no current fixed 256-row cluster cap.
Ordinary queries and kernels include staging and cluster stores through the same mask/range traversal. Exact cluster selection requires clean maintenance and scans metadata; it does not build a neighbor index. Sparse maintenance still copies identity-capacity keys and scans store metadata, so classifying only dirty identities does not make total maintenance O(dirty identities).
The thesis’s memory blocks and historical bounded partitions explain the design lineage. Current growth and reclamation follow decision 0014, which supersedes 0013. The rejected special Cluster component in 0007 is not part of placement. Partition reports retain measurements with their layout and revision labels.
Implementation: Source, Source, Source. Evidence: test/spatial_test.mojo, test/partitioned_spatial_test.mojo, test/gpu_spatial_test.mojo. For the application boundary, use Maintain particle locality.

data: A logical archetype groups entities with identical component composition. A physical store holds one contiguous row collection for that composition. We keep component masks in a lazy transition graph; its nodes name canonical dense stores. Partitioned locality can add several physical stores beneath the same logical node. An internal Archetype value represents a physical store, so its name alone does not imply one store per component combination.
data.columns-contain-component-values#Columns:
The memory diagram shows one store with Position and Velocity active.
Scroll horizontally to read the full figure.
Columns separate component types; fields remain together inside each value.
The typed component table tracks a mask, live length, shared capacity, per-column revisions, and store incarnation (a fresh number for each new store). Its fixed component-ID-indexed array contains column descriptors. Each active descriptor owns an optional allocation and type-specific lifecycle functions; inactive descriptors have no component allocation. Entity IDs have a separate allocation. Columns and IDs share row indices, but their allocations are independent.
Position.x and Position.y are fields in each Position struct. They are not two scalar columns. The same applies to Velocity.dx/dy. Spare capacity is uninitialized storage, not live component objects. The diagram’s boxes describe ownership and indexing, not header offsets, pointer packing, a stable ABI, or a CPU SIMD-batch API. In particular, the thesis’s pointer-slot sketch must not be read as today’s descriptor layout.
data.structural-transitions-and-identity#Stru:
Adding a component changes logical composition. The destination is the canonical store for the new mask, including when the source is a cluster store. In partition mode that destination stages rows until maintenance. The diagram follows particle B while particle C fills its old row.
Scroll horizontally to read the full figure.
B keeps its identity while its location changes; C’s location changes too.
Before touching initialized storage, _ComponentMigration separates retained, removed, replaced, and added types, and checks missing removals or overlapping additions. Retained values move without destruction at the old location. Removed and replaced values stay initialized until destruction; new values initialize the destination. Swap-removal then repairs the source hole without destroying already moved values a second time. Typed row-permutation validation also completes before its first swap. These checks are not a promise of transactional rollback for arbitrary allocation failure.
Entity is an ID/generation pair. The entity pool tracks liveness and recycling; _entity_locations[id] maps a live identity to physical-store index and row. All row movement repairs that mapping, including the tail row used by swap-removal. A copied handle survives relocation, whereas an external component reference cannot survive a structural change or spatial maintenance. An ID from one world is not a cross-world reference.
Implementation: Source, Source, Source, Source, Source. Evidence: test/host_storage_lifecycle_test.mojo, test/partitioned_spatial_test.mojo; decision 0009 records movement guarantees.
data.typed-lifecycles#Typed lifecycles:
Host components satisfy ComponentType (Copyable & Deinitable); they can own heap data. _ComponentColumn erases the concrete type while retaining typed operations for copying, moving, destroying, swapping, and allocating values.
Operation Treatment of live values Copy a store Copy-construct each initialized value into independent column storage. Grow capacity Allocate typed storage, move live values into it, then release the old allocation. Remove a row Destroy removed values and move the last row into the hole when necessary. Permute rows Swap entity IDs and every active component column together, preserving owners. Destroy a store Destroy its live values once, then release column allocations. Raw byte transfer is a separate device eligibility boundary; support for an owning host component does not make that component device-safe or eligible for threaded host work. See the execution contracts.

data: AtomicValue and Synchronized own target-local state. Their copyable views retain one protection identity; owners and acquired guards are noncopyable. These standalone primitives do not supply KernelContext.sync, collection domains, automatic transfer bindings, or deferred retries. Those parts of accepted decision 0016 are unimplemented; decision 0017 remains proposed. Coordinate shared writes explains available application patterns.
data.allocation-and-lifetime-boundary#Allocat:
Unsafe view construction borrows existing storage; it neither allocates nor transfers it. Device payload and state must already be device-accessible, aligned, initialized, and retained until all work completes. Host and device allocations are separate protection domains. Explicit move/destruction methods keep borrowed views from passing ordinary resource/capture raw-byte checks, including when nested in aggregates.
Structural lock bits preserve row addresses; resource leases preserve source lifetimes; synchronization state coordinates concurrent data access. None of those mechanisms substitutes for the others. Adapter capability declarations also do not add synchronization automatically.
Implementation: Source. Evidence: test/synchronization_test.mojo, test/check_synchronization_contracts.py, test/gpu_synchronization_test.mojo, Apple publication research.
data.one-state-word-per-protected-payload#One:
Synchronized stores a payload and one initialized UInt32 state word. Zero means unlocked, the high bit (0x80000000) means one writer, and the remaining bits count readers up to 0x7fffffff. Every view of an overlapping payload must use the same state word.
try_read loads state, rejects writer/saturation, and makes at most one strong CAS to increment readers. try_write makes one CAS from zero to the writer bit. Successful acquisition uses acquire ordering. A changed value or failed CAS returns Busy; there is no spin loop, fairness, lock upgrade, or blocking wait. The caller decides what to do with unfinished work.
A successful TryAccess owns a guard until it is consumed or destroyed. take transfers that guard. Guard borrows confine payload references; release stores zero for a writer or atomically decrements readers, with release ordering. Scope exit releases access during error unwinding; it does not undo payload writes.
data.scalar-operations-and-scope#Scalar opera:
AtomicView points to aligned UInt32 or Int32 storage accessed only atomically. Add/subtract wrap at the scalar width and return the previous value. Strong compare-exchange returns success and the observed value, using relaxed failure ordering. Read views permit loads only. Scalar operations default to relaxed ordering: counters do not publish adjacent ordinary payload writes.
The implementation selects CPU-wide scope, NVIDIA device scope, or AMD agent scope. Loads accept acquire and stores accept release. Supported read-modify-write operations also accept acquire, release, and acquire-release. Apple GPU support is limited to relaxed add/subtract and relaxed/acquire loads or relaxed/release stores. Strong CAS, ordered updates, and guards are rejected there. Release stores and acquire loads supply the separately verified Apple publication path; a compile probe alone would not prove hardware ordering.

data: A ResourceStorage owns one source value per resource type. An invocation validates its Resources declarations, leases the sources, and retains prepared views until completion. Leases reject reentrant lookup, replacement, or removal of bound sources. They protect lifetime; they do not synchronize workers or repair escaped aliases.
data.device-copy-validity#Device-copy validit:
Buffer capacity reuse is independent of content reuse. By default, readable inputs upload every invocation. Experimental World.reuse_device_copies also retains successful transfer records, as the figure shows.
Scroll horizontally to read the full figure.
Skipping uploads requires matching validity metadata; output publication stays eager.
Resource revisions come from an increasing storage counter. Mutable get, add/set, declared host writes, and successful device writes advance them; read does not. Reuse still validates and leases the source. A current read-only adapted copy can skip prepare_device; mutable adapted sources always prepare and never reuse their contents.
A column record identifies storage identity, physical-store slot, never-reused store incarnation, column revision, first row, row count, and packed offset. A mutation, row movement, reclaimed-slot replacement, or changed packing offset invalidates the relevant match. Written outputs still download. Failed calls invalidate touched records; disabling reuse, removal, and copying a world discard relevant records. Moves preserve owned state.
Tracked mutable exposure invalidates conservatively before the caller writes. A later edit through an escaped reference or raw pointer cannot advance the counter automatically: it requires explicit invalidation. Revisions are validity metadata, not alias tracking or a promise of persistent device-only state.
Implementation: Source, Source, Source, Source. Evidence: test/resource_adapter_test.mojo, test/mutable_resource_adapter_test.mojo, test/device_copy_reuse_test.mojo, test/device_column_reuse_test.mojo. The resource reference defines author obligations and the copy-reuse guide shows invalidation.
data.packing-and-publication#Packing and publ:
Component access declarations determine the transfer directions in this adaptation of the thesis’s device-memory figure.
Scroll horizontally to read the full figure.
Read access supplies input; write access schedules output publication.
Readable columns upload each selected span to its packed offset. Write-only columns allocate output without uploading old bytes, so kernels must set every processed row. After execution, only declared written columns download and scatter back. Resource and explicit-capture outputs use the same invocation queue. Selection gaps stay untouched.
_TransferFrame snapshots uploads in native host buffers and retains download staging buffers with eventual host destinations. Queued copies therefore do not retain caller-owned upload memory. The executor synchronizes the queue, publishes staged bytes, commits resource/column records, then finalizes adapters. Errors drain submitted work before releasing owners. If completion cannot be confirmed, the world becomes unusable for further execution. Already performed host writes and published outputs are not rolled back.
data.sources-and-target-local-views#Sources a:
Ordinary resources bind directly on the host. Device transfer accepts only supported plain representations. Recursive field checks reject owning, pointer-bearing, or nontrivial values; PlainValue permits an author-declared opaque representation only after trivial copy/move/destruction checks. That declaration makes the author responsible for pointer-free nested data.
A DevicePassableResource source instead declares a stateless ResourceAdapter. Its host view borrows source data; its device view refers to adapter-managed target allocations. read selects View[False]; write and read_write select View[True]. Mutable preparation distinguishes fresh initialized output from preserved contents. It runs once per invocation before any range/chunk/launch, and finalization runs once after successful execution/publication, including empty matches. Mutable access requires adapter capability flags; threaded and device mutation also require concurrent-mutation support.
Read-only adapters guarantee concurrent readability of their views and reachable data. Owning sources stay on the host; copying their pointer bytes would not transfer the owned allocation. This is why a portable buffer or grid has a separate kernel representation.

data:
We change ECS contracts through the existing requirements and ADR workflow, then verify implementation, examples, and measured costs together.
Task or lookup Material Set up, build, and test Locked environments, package builds, focused checks, and platform failures. Test and hardware coverage Compile contracts, sanitizer/debug markers, and the meaning of a hardware skip. Change an ECS contract Existing design records, implementation evidence, benchmark obligations, and documentation. Build documentation and figures Compiler JSON, Modo, checked excerpts, Hugo, API verification, and reproducible assets. Measure an implementation change Workloads, timing boundaries, paired samples, and retained evidence. Operate regression checks Baselines, case manifests, thresholds, confirmation, and failure reports. Design and evidence map Repository requirements, ADR statuses, research, coding standards, and historical material. Measurement reports Scoped investigations with hardware/compiler/revision and limitations. The architecture explanations describe current mechanisms. Tasks and priorities remain in the roadmap; completed releases remain in the changelog.

Use representative workloads to compare a storage, query, movement, or execution change. We validate semantic equivalence before interpreting elapsed time; application profiling starts in Measure and tune a simulation.
data.benchmark-methodology#Benchmark methodol:
Build a focused manual driver once with pixi run mojo build -I src benchmark/<benchmark_filename>.mojo -o /tmp/larecs-benchmark, then run /tmp/larecs-benchmark repeatedly. Run the complete manual suite with pixi run mojo run -I src benchmark/run_benchmarks.mojo.
When changing storage, queries, classification, row movement, or execution costs, add or update representative benchmarks using these criteria:
Keep the combined PR performance checks near one minute per runner, including compilation, warmup, and sampling. Measure cold compilation and execution separately on Linux and macOS before expanding the suite. Keep large worlds, GPU cases, and the complete benchmark registry in focused manual drivers. Use deterministic inputs, bounded calibration or fixed iteration counts, and a compact scenario matrix. Spatial cases should cover uniform, dense, sparse, and moving entities with different maintenance cadences. Compare identical entities and semantic work, with an unchanged-layout control. Measure isolated operations and complete frames when useful. Include input updates, classification, sorting, movement, location repair, and transfers whenever they belong to the claimed workload. State excluded setup and maintenance costs; validate results, locations, and payload preservation outside the timer, and consume results to prevent dead-code elimination. Build each timing binary once, then run it repeatedly. Compare the same current driver against baseline and current libraries on the same runner with matching compiler versions and optimization settings. Use optimized builds without debug info, sanitizers, or tracing. Run builds and measurements sequentially, with no competing benchmark jobs, and report compilation separately. Warm both binaries, alternate baseline/current order, and use repeated paired samples. Keep machine-specific timing baselines out of the repository. See PR performance checks and spatial checks for baseline selection, thresholds, confirmation, and support for revisions predating the spatial API. Keep the small regression checks in pixi run tests test on Linux and macOS; focused test-file runs omit performance checks. Investigate sustained failures and document evidence before changing thresholds; use dedicated measurements for smaller regressions. Keep scenario matrices and expected-case manifests synchronized. Invalid or incomplete reports, build failures, and correctness failures must fail checks. Update the regression reference when changing cases, timing boundaries, sampling, or baseline selection. Record hardware, compiler, method, and limitations with performance claims; track unmeasured benefits and remaining work in the roadmap.
data.focused-driver-selection#Focused driver: Mechanism Checked driver and evidence Exact selections and structural batches benchmark/entity_selection_benchmark.mojo; selection reports. Implemented threaded engine benchmark/threaded_execution.mojo; threaded report. Scalar atomics and uncontended guards benchmark/synchronization_benchmark.mojo; protocol and limits. Dirty classification benchmark/dirty_spatial.mojo; deferred maintenance report. Growable partition placement benchmark/partitioned_spatial.mojo; current and historical layouts. Ordinary and adapted resources benchmark/resource_execution_benchmark.mojo and benchmark/resource_adapter_benchmark.mojo; resource report. For a new comparison, retain hardware/OS, compiler build, both library revisions, driver hash, flags, warmup/calibration, paired raw samples, correctness results, and excluded costs. If a historical record lacks a field, label it unknown rather than reconstructing a claim from a machine name. Keep timing reports separate from application instructions and from the roadmap’s unfinished work.

data:
These checks establish different facts. A rejected program checks a compiler
contract; a host test checks host execution; successful device compilation
does not establish actual accelerator execution.
data.compile-contract-commands#Compile-contra:
Run these commands from the repository root in the test environment. Positive controls must compile, negative controls must fail for the expected diagnostic, and intentional exclusions must remain accepted.
Contract Command Type-only struct invariants and exclusions pixi run -e test python test/check_struct_constraints.py Iterator mutability, filters, and borrows pixi run -e test python test/check_iteration_contracts.py Explicit backend selection and unsupported combinations pixi run -e test python test/check_execution_backend_contracts.py Threaded eligibility, captures, resource access, and fallback pixi run -e test python test/check_threaded_contracts.py Ordinary/adapted resource representations and capabilities pixi run -e test python test/check_resource_contracts.py Synchronization view/guard confinement and backend restrictions pixi run -e test python test/check_synchronization_contracts.py Read-only spatial registration filters pixi run spatial-filter-checks Duplicate resource/type-list fixtures pixi run test-resource-compile-failures The full pixi run tests test wrapper runs the first seven families and the thread-capacity Python tests. Focused world_entity_iterator, execution_backend, threaded_execution, resource_adapter, and synchronization test files trigger their corresponding family. The last table row is separate. The struct checker uses type-only bindings so constructor checks cannot conceal a missing declaration invariant; see the constraint audit.
data.markers-and-diagnostics#Markers and diag:
test/run_tests.sh enables ASAN, -g, -DASSERT=all, and Tracy linkage. # SKIP_ASAN opts a file out of sanitization; # SKIP_DEBUG omits debug info. Every test that launches a GPU kernel needs # SKIP_DEBUG because of the Metal compiler failure. Neither marker means that the test may skip its assertions. The doctest runner uses assertions and Tracy linkage, but does not enable the test wrapper’s ASAN/debug defaults.
CI bounds test compilation concurrency with --parallel 2 and retains output/memory/ diagnostics. An interrupted runner or missing artifact is not a correctness pass. See the CI workflow and the memory monitor for the recorded process boundary; keep performance measurements isolated from builds.
data.runtime-evidence#Runtime evidence:
Result What it establishes Compile pass for device code The installed compiler accepts that specialization; no hardware behavior is proved. Host correctness pass Assertions ran on the host, including actual worker overlap where a test checks it. Device SKIP, or an early guard returning before a launch Host/setup or compile coverage only; no device execution. A device launch completes and output assertions pass Execution on the named device for that workload and toolchain. has_accelerator() describes compilation support. Runtime context creation can still fail. The particle programs probe both and print explicit device PASS or SKIP evidence. Some older GPU tests return early on unsupported targets while the file still reports PASS; inspect the guard and logs, rather than counting file passes as device coverage. ExecutionBackend.DEVICE itself has no host fallback.
Record compiler/build, OS, processor/device, revision, executed path, assertions, and skips separately. The Linux/macOS CI matrix does not imply NVIDIA, AMD, or Apple device coverage merely from runner names. A source or driver change can invalidate earlier evidence; current status is in the compatibility reference, and durable backend investigations remain in the evidence map.

data:
Use this workflow when a change affects ownership, storage, query membership, execution, safety, compatibility, or measured costs. It follows the existing repository guidelines and ADR workflow.
Locate the current requirement and relevant decisions in the design map. Check status and supersession before treating a decision as current. Verify behavior in src/larecs and focused tests; acceptance alone does not prove implementation. For a consequential choice, add the next numbered file in docs/design/decisions/ using the index’s metadata schema and Context, Decision, Rationale, Consequences, and Evidence sections. Mark unaccepted ideas proposed. To replace an accepted choice, retain the old record, mark it superseded, and update the index and requirements. Update implementation and representative correctness/compile-contract tests together. For row movement, preserve typed lifecycles, live identities, location repair, bounded membership, and invalidation. For execution, check fallback, empty matches, cleanup, binding lifetime, and unsupported targets. Use architecture to trace affected mechanisms. Add or update representative benchmarks for changes to storage, queries, classification, movement, or execution costs. Follow the methodology and regression operation; a passing broad threshold does not prove zero overhead. Update visible application consequences in guides, exact contracts in the reference/docstrings, and changed mechanisms in architecture. Extract runnable listings from checked sources, regenerate affected figures, and run the documentation build. Keep unfinished tasks and priorities in the roadmap, and completed release history in the changelog. Research notes and thesis alternatives remain evidence with their original status; they do not create a second requirements or documentation-policy system. The canonical coding standards also govern listings and API docstrings.

The canonical records stay at their repository paths. Links here resolve at the same revision as the generated API, preserving front matter, supersession, cross-links, and durable evidence. We do not infer implementation from acceptance.
Source Authority and use Design index Complete ADR index, lifecycle meanings, metadata schema, and recording workflow. ECS requirements Accepted contracts with evidence and explicit implementation gaps. Repository architecture map Source-level overview; published architecture expands current mechanisms. Development reference Canonical coding/docstring standards and detailed platform workarounds. Glossary Shared terminology for composition, storage, execution, and ownership. Roadmap Unfinished work and priorities. Changelog Completed release history.
data.decisions#Decisions:
The statuses below identify how to read the records; qualifications in their front matter remain authoritative. Current behavior is checked against source and tests in architecture.
Records Status and boundary 0001 selections, 0002 device execution, 0003 grid stride, 0004 errors Accepted; current selection/execution foundations. 0005 spatial ordering, 0010 full maintenance Superseded by 0012; retain historical classification/movement rationale. 0006 partitions, 0008 dirty identities, 0009 typed movement, 0012 deferred maintenance Accepted; current spatial foundations. 0007 special Cluster component Rejected; not a component users must add. 0011 regression checks Accepted; gate operation describes the implemented checker. 0013 bounded blocks Superseded by 0014; the historical 256-row cap is not current. 0014 growable stores Accepted; current partition layout. 0015 terminology Superseded by 0023; preserves beta spelling migration. 0016 synchronization Accepted, partially implemented; standalone primitives exist, dedicated kernel bindings and collection domains do not. 0017 deferred access Proposed; no callable deferred-access API. 0018 adapters Superseded by 0020 and extended by 0022; preserve source/view and lifetime rationale. 0019 threaded execution Superseded by 0020; its feasibility evidence is historical. 0020 plain values Accepted; threaded execution remains experimental. 0021 device-copy reuse, 0022 mutable adapters Accepted, experimental; implemented contracts are checked against transfer and adapter tests. 0023 explicit targets, 0024 storage ranges Accepted; current target selection and bounded ranges.
data.research-and-historical-evidence#Researc:
Research describes the revision and question it investigated. Old on_device spellings, mutable-adapter experiments, or a recommended design are not current APIs. A probe may depend on its recorded toolchain rather than the current one.
Repository evidence Scope Host-thread investigation Feasibility findings and prototype measurements; not the implemented engine. Companion dispatch probe and benchmark retain that experiment. GPU synchronization survey Upstream primitive/backend evidence supporting 0016, with coverage limitations. Apple publication ordering M4 correctness/performance evidence for release-store/acquire-load publication. Storage range migration Cursor-sharing evidence and timing samples affected by concurrent builds; no controlled speedup claim. Struct constraint audit Mojo 1.0 declaration invariants, proof limits, and intentional exclusions. Reference invalidation probe Escaped-reference behavior motivating explicit device-copy invalidation. Resource-view probe, trait-dispatch probe Resource descriptor and trait-dispatch experiments; production behavior comes from current adapters/tests. Measurement reports preserve historical benchmark material with its environment, method, and missing metadata called out. Thesis figures supply visual vocabulary; their adaptation is recorded in the figure catalog. Thesis-specific systems, memory headers, bounded layouts, or branch experiments establish no current Larecs guarantee.

data: Run the publishing checks after changing a page, example, API contract, or figure. Work from the repository root with the locked setup. The pipeline retains Modo; mojo doc supplies declarations, Modo extracts examples and generates Markdown, and Hugo renders the site.
data.add-a-checked-excerpt#Add a checked exce:
Keep a complete program with result assertions under examples/particles/. Mark one coherent excerpt with # region NAME and # endregion NAME, then include it and offer the full program:
{{</* example file="particles/movement.mojo" region="kernel" */>}} {{</* example file="particles/movement.mojo" full=true */>}} The runner includes all particle programs and automatically includes referenced programs elsewhere under examples/. Missing files, missing/empty/unbalanced regions, unchecked inline Mojo fences, and missing entry points fail. Keep required types, filters, kernels, and systems visible before explaining them. Short standalone inline examples may use Modo’s labelled doctest blocks; global=true requires a complete def main() raises:. Hide imports only.
data.build-and-verify#Build and verify:
Run the publishing command before committing a documentation change:
pixi run verify-docs The command performs these checks:
Clear generated Markdown and tests, regenerate compiler JSON, and run Modo with strict coverage and cross-reference checks. Compare the source-derived doctest inventory with every extracted file. Compile and execute all extracted tests, all particle stages, and every program referenced by an example shortcode. There is no exclusion list. Verify backend, resource/type-list, and spatial-registration rejection diagnostics with the existing compiler-contract checks. Their valid controls and the checked spatial stage must still compile. Re-export every non-helper figure to a temporary directory and reject differences from the committed SVGs. Build Hugo into an empty destination. Check every symbol/source target, root export, ordinary site link, repository evidence path, image, anchor, legacy redirect, and indexed search destination. Exercise failure fixtures and a second deployment prefix. Chromium checks search navigation, retained redirect fragments, mobile navigation, 360/768/1440-pixel layouts, expanded long declarations, and SVG canvases in both themes. Requests are served from generated files through browser interception; no server or live website is required. Delete generated outputs and regenerate compiler JSON, Markdown, tests, metadata, and HTML. Require byte-identical files at the same revision and base URL. Programs execute once; the second extraction must match the files that executed. pixi run build-docs runs steps 1–5 for a shorter edit cycle. Use pixi run --manifest-path scripts/pixi.toml test-docs to rerun integration fixtures after a build. The published files are in docs/site/public/. Generated JSON, Markdown, tests, and HTML are disposable outputs; commit the source pages, templates, programs, figure sources, and SVG exports.
The example log and output/docs/examples.json record actual device execution separately from hardware skips. A successful compilation or host assertion is not device coverage. Set DOCS_REQUIRE_DEVICE=1 before either build command on an accelerator machine to reject skips. CI can publish host-checked docs without claiming accelerator execution. Browser screenshots and layout evidence are in output/docs/browser/; inspect labels and captions there when a figure or stylesheet changes. Automated checks cannot judge an explanation’s clarity.
data.export-figures-and-inspect-the-site#Expo:
Edit the self-contained Typst/CeTZ sources, then update their exports:
pixi run figures pixi run verify-docs The figure build pins CeTZ 0.5.2, uses --ignore-system-fonts with committed Inter fonts, and exports every non-helper docs/figures/*.typ. Commit each source and docs/site/static/images/<name>.svg together. Keep its caption, alt text, and interpretation aligned. SVGs retain a light canvas in both themes and scroll within the reading column on narrow screens. The figure catalog records provenance.
Use pixi run serve-docs after a build, or pixi run watch-docs while editing. The watch loop supports iteration; verify-docs is the publishing gate. Repository PR previews use https://larecs.github.io/larecs/pr-preview/pr-<number>/ through the publishing workflow.
data.keep-links-and-incoming-urls-working#Kee:
Use api for symbols, built-site paths for pages, and repo for repository records outside docs/src. Repository/source/example links use the checkout’s HEAD revision; publish a committed checkout. Keep the initializer’s Exports: list aligned with imports. Inherited or compiler-synthesized members link to their owning source declaration.
Guide compatibility routes and heading IDs are checked against the incoming-URL fixture. Generated API aliases also retain method and overload fragments. On a case-sensitive host, System/ redirects independently of the system/ module. On a case-insensitive filesystem, the module landing page handles the legacy capitalized URL without overwriting its own content. Keep these checks when changing paths; a redirect must preserve both the base URL and incoming hash.
data.keep-warnings-fatal#Keep warnings fatal:
Strict checks now apply to the complete generated tree. Missing alias/field descriptions and malformed cross-references were repaired before enabling Modo’s strict: true. Declarations are URL-encoded between Modo and Hugo so compiler-generated backticks cannot become false cross-references; the exact compiler declaration remains available. The wrapper rejects Modo errors, documentation warnings, and hook failures even when the packaged Linux launcher returns zero. Hugo also runs with --panicOnWarning; the wrapper rejects its template warnings.
All eight historical doctest exclusions are retired:
Former label or source Checked replacement or retirement HostStorage_add_entity_comps HostStorage_add_entity asserts individual creation. HostStorage_add_query_comps HostStorage_add_components checks filtered batch addition. HostStorage_remove_query_comps HostStorage_remove_components checks filtered batch removal. HostStorage_apply The commented historical example is no longer generated; current mutation uses the checked structural-change guide. Query_query_init Removed Query API; the queries/iteration doctest checks the current locked range. Query_query_without Removed Query API; the same checked guide covers exclusion filters. larecs_readme The shared particle program replaces the duplicated introduction example. Scheduler_scheduler The scheduler doctest now has a complete main and executes. A partially missing extraction fails as well as an empty directory. New warnings must be fixed in the source or renderer; do not add a warning baseline or omit a program to make the build pass.
data.prepare-the-generation-environment#Prepa:
Install the root and documentation environments, then the pinned Chromium build:
pixi install --locked pixi install --locked --manifest-path scripts/pixi.toml pixi run --manifest-path scripts/pixi.toml playwright install chromium Generation supports Linux x86-64 and macOS Apple Silicon. pixi.lock pins Mojo, MAX, and tracing dependencies; scripts/pixi.lock pins Python, Modo, Hugo, Typst, Playwright, and the native macOS Go toolchain. Linux CI uses Ubuntu 24.04, supported by the pinned Playwright release, and installs Chromium’s system libraries with playwright install --with-deps chromium. On Apple Silicon, the wrapper builds the installed Modo release natively and caches it under scripts/.pixi/; Linux uses its bundled executable.

data: This reference describes scripts/check_performance.py and its bounded CPU suites. Run commands from the repository root after setup. The methodology governs new cases; historical gate costs are measurements, not runtime promises.
data.pr-to-pr-performance-checks#PR-to-PR per:
pixi run performance-check --base <revision> compares the current library with another Git revision on the same machine. Without --base, local runs compare the working tree against committed HEAD; GitHub PR runs use the exact PR base SHA, and main-branch push runs use the previous push commit. The tested current revision is the checkout SHA (normally the PR merge commit in CI). The complete pixi run tests test command runs the gate on Linux and macOS following correctness tests. Focused test-file runs omit it.
The coordinator builds the same current driver against both source trees with the installed Mojo compiler, using optimized builds without tracing, debug information, or sanitizers. It warms both binaries, then runs five pairs, alternating baseline/current order. A case becomes a candidate only if four pairs and the paired medians show over 30% slowdown and over 500 ns extra operation/frame time. Candidates are checked in a fresh five-pair round; only candidates recurring in both rounds fail. Invalid/incomplete reports, incorrect results, compilation failures, unavailable baselines, and timeouts fail rather than silently skipping coverage.
The two focused drivers avoid the expensive complete benchmark registry:
Core case Sizes Timed work Excluded setup and validation access 512/2,048 matching rows Stable-ID component reads and integer checksum World construction; exact per-entity payload checks query 512/2,048 matching rows Fresh filtered iterator, row visits, and checksum Construction of two matching archetypes and equally many excluded tag-only rows; payload checks execute 512/2,048 rows Ordinary host dispatch and integer increments Construction; check every row’s accumulated increments selected_execute 64 selected rows amid 512/2,048 background rows Host dispatch over a reusable contiguous selection Construction and selection creation/release; selected and untouched-row checks selected_mutation Same selection/background sizes Add/remove a tag, including partial-archetype movement and location repair Construction; final membership, absence of tags, payload, and background-location checks batch_cycle 512/2,048 rows Batch creation, payload initialization, removal, and recycling World construction and first validation/warmup cycle; recycled payload, membership, and surviving control-row checks Core calibration doubles from 8 to at most 8,192 operations, stopping at 5 ms per case. Fast cases can reach the cap first. Each duration is per complete operation, not per entity. Read cases consume the checksum inside the timer; execution writes are checked after timing, with observable lengths consumed inside the timer. Spatial timing boundaries and the case matrix are below.
Run one driver with pixi run core-benchmarks or pixi run spatial-benchmarks. Select a gate with pixi run performance-check --suite core --base <revision> or --suite spatial; repeat --suite to select multiple drivers. The original pixi run spatial-performance-check remains a spatial-only compatibility command.
Reports default to the ignored output/performance/ directory; use --output to choose another directory. report.json includes the schema version, requested/resolved/effective baselines, current checkout SHA and dirty state, driver SHA-256 hashes, compiler, OS/CPU, thresholds, compilation and sampling costs, all paired measurements, and both confirmation rounds when needed. summary.md gives median times, paired changes, candidates, and confirmed failures. Candidates whose confirmation did not finish are labeled unconfirmed; only a completed confirmation can label a candidate transient. Process logs retain build, warmup, execution, and error diagnostics. GitHub adds the Markdown to the job summary and uploads the reports/logs as performance-<runner>-<attempt> artifacts for 30 days, including failed checks. This uses read-only PR permissions and works without publishing PR comments. Require the existing build/test checks in branch protection to enforce the gate.
There are no checked-in machine-specific golden timings. Driver changes affect both sides; compare historical evidence only when hashes and environments are compatible. Compiler upgrades do not measure compiler-to-compiler changes. These broad thresholds target substantial regressions on shared runners; smaller or cumulative regressions, larger worlds, heap-backed payloads, disjoint selections, and device costs need focused measurements or future coverage. See decision 0011 and the roadmap.
data.small-spatial-benchmarks-on-every-pr#Sma:
Run pixi run spatial-benchmarks for one bounded CPU-only comparison, or pixi run spatial-performance-check --base <revision> for a regression check. The complete pixi run tests test command runs this suite through the shared coordinator after successful correctness tests, on both Linux and macOS PR runners. Focused test-file runs omit it. The existing 100,000-row maintenance benchmark and the full benchmark suite remain manual measurements.
The small driver uses 512 and 2,048 entities, one archetype, an integer cell key and a 128-byte SIMD payload per row. It inserts rows in a deterministic scrambled order, then compares the same stable-ID cell visits before and after spatial ordering. Its 32 cases cover:
Workload Cell distribution Timed work Static cell aggregates Uniform: 8 entities/cell Read keys and all payload lanes; sum and square each cell’s aggregate Static cell aggregates Dense: 64 entities/cell Same operation, with fewer occupied cells Static cell aggregates Sparse: 8 entities/cell, key gaps of 1,024 Same operation across nonconsecutive occupied keys Maintenance alone All three distributions Clean explicit boundary, or reverse keys via stable-ID access and sort/move/repair every pass Moving cell aggregates Uniform Update every entity’s cell, aggregate cells, maintain every frame or every fourth frame Static workload timing excludes construction, registration, and the initial maintenance pass. Mobile timing includes input updates and the selected maintenance cadence; its scrambled control performs the same updates and cell visits without maintenance. Maintenance-only reversal and conservative marking via mutable stable-ID access are included in timing. A clean ordered boundary uses deferred maintenance in the current library and full classification in older baseline libraries. This is an intentional maintenance-contract change; use the dedicated dirty-classification report for an explicit full-scan control. Checksums validate aggregate results and payload preservation, and a query validates maintenance’s output order, outside the timer. These are synthetic cell aggregates; full neighborhood algorithms, additional archetypes, transfer costs, and larger working sets remain separate measurements.
Each batch doubles from 8 to at most 8,192 frames, stopping once it takes 20 ms. The checker compiles the same current driver against the current library and the PR’s base commit, warms both binaries, then collects five paired runs with alternating execution order. It reports median frame times and paired changes for both ordered and scrambled controls. A case fails only when at least four pairs show both over 30% slowdown and over 500 ns extra time, and the paired medians exceed those thresholds. A suspected regression must recur in a fresh five-pair run. This broad threshold catches substantial regressions on shared runners; smaller changes need dedicated measurements. No machine-specific timing baseline is checked in.
The baseline comes from the GitHub PR event’s base SHA. Local runs default to committed HEAD; pass --base to compare another revision. An unavailable full SHA is fetched over public HTTPS. Since release PR #174 predates the spatial API, spatial PR #175 bootstraps against 42234f3b43d4dda58a674842374115f78ec2f08d, the implementation before this benchmark addition. Subsequent PRs whose base has the spatial API use their actual base. Compilation, malformed/missing records, checksum failures, and sustained regressions all fail the check.

These scoped records retain benchmark investigations and their limitations. They describe the recorded hardware, toolchain, revision, and workload rather than promising application performance. Missing metadata is identified explicitly. Use the methodology for new measurements and the regression reference for current gate operation.

This is a dynamically regenerated comparison, not one fixed historical run. The workflow records its checkout SHA and resolves Mojo through benchmark/plots/pixi.lock; its ubuntu-24.04 label does not identify a CPU or cache size. No numerical speedup is asserted without a selected run’s data. The driver defines iteration calibration and measured work; compiler generation, world construction, plotting, and dependency setup are outside per-entity loop timing. Hosted load, changing runner hardware, and artifact retention limit cross-run interpretation.
data.versus-array-of-structs#Versus Array of:
The publishing-run plots show iteration time per entity for a workload that adds velocity to position in both dimensions. Historical driver fields are not the tutorial’s API: the checked particle example uses Position.x/y and Velocity.dx/dy. See the plotting driver for its exact data types.
The benchmark is performed with different amounts of “payload components”, where each of them has two Float64 fields, just like Position and Velocity. Further, the total number of entities is varied from 100 to 1 million.
Plots and raw data are available in the aos-benchmark artifact of the publishing run that produced them. Select the run for the measured checkout SHA; the report contains no fixed checked-in plot or golden timings.
The documentation workflow (.github/workflows/publish.yml) regenerates this plot for each published commit on a GitHub-hosted ubuntu-24.04 runner, using the Mojo version pinned in benchmark/plots/pixi.lock. The workflow does not record the runner’s CPU or cache sizes, and the hardware behind that runner label can change between runs. Read the plot as a comparison on one machine, not as a prediction for other hardware. Each run keeps the raw results as its aos-benchmark artifact. To measure your own machine, run pixi run plots in benchmark/plots.

data: This report retains M4 results for implementation 76868ef based on 0241e91, with Mojo 1.0.0 (ed45d567). The original run did not record an OS build. The current maintenance mechanism can differ from this measured revision; the workloads and timing exclusions follow below. “Current” below refers to the measured implementation.
data.deferred-dirty-classification#Deferred d:
Build pixi run mojo build -I src benchmark/dirty_spatial.mojo -o /tmp/larecs-dirty-spatial, then run that binary with no concurrent compilation or benchmark jobs. It constructs identical scrambled 2,048/32,768-entity worlds with 72 component bytes per row plus entity IDs, establishes initial spatial order, warms both paths, and alternates five paired samples of sixteen frames (1,024 frames for clean boundaries to resolve their small cost). The 24 scenarios cover uniform (16 entities/cell), dense (256/cell), and sparse (16/cell with key gaps of 128) distributions, with 0, 1, 1/64, or all identities updated. Each updated identity receives two reference writes per frame; classification observes final values. On alternating frames those writes cancel. Other frames advance cells by one. Both paths perform identical updates and semantic work.
The deferred path uses automatic tracking. Its control requests a full rebuild after those same writes. Timings include updates, marking, key scratch allocation, classification, sorting, typed movement of all columns, and location repair. Construction, registration, initial maintenance, and correctness checks are excluded. Every sample validates complete key order, each identity/location, the expected final input for every identity, and all eight payload lanes outside timing through read-only queries. Output records rows, distribution, dirty count, pair number, and deferred/full frame ns. This compares current deferred maintenance with current explicit full rebuilds; it does not measure a historical implementation or total application speedup.
Clean calls do no row work. Dirty calls still copy O(entity-ID capacity) keys and inspect affected archetypes, so sparse classification is not O(D) complete maintenance. Full rebuilds currently reset sparse membership and caches. Dense updates may favor contiguous full classification; structural-heavy workloads use full rebuilds. Retained keys/membership cost at least nine bytes per allocated ID plus queue capacity (full ID/generation identities and allocator slack). Scratch and movement metadata add temporary memory. These are layout costs, not measured application memory usage.
A local run on Apple M4, arm64, Mojo 1.0.0 (ed45d567) with implementation 76868ef (based on 0241e91) built the optimized driver in 4.74 seconds. Five warmed pairs gave these median complete-frame times for 32,768 entities:
Distribution Dirty identities Deferred Explicit full rebuild Deferred/full Uniform 1 0.685 ms 1.076 ms 0.637 Uniform 512 0.749 ms 1.133 ms 0.661 Dense 512 0.811 ms 1.194 ms 0.679 Sparse 1 0.097 ms 0.490 ms 0.198 Sparse 512 0.112 ms 0.497 ms 0.226 Uniform 32,768 0.850 ms 0.858 ms 0.991 Across both sizes and all distributions, nonzero sparse-update scenarios took 19.5–67.9% of the full-rebuild frame time. Clean boundaries measured approximately 3–4 ns (close to timer resolution), versus 0.031/0.490 ms full rebuilds at the two sizes. Fully dirty frames took 99.1–104.6% of the explicit control. An earlier version that resolved every dirty identity separately took 131–141% for fully dirty frames; the accepted all-ID-dirty fallback avoids that column/location setup cost. Neither path can avoid moving clean rows when regrouping demands it.
The separate same-driver PR gate against 0241e91 passed all 12 core and 32 spatial cases in 41.1 seconds including four sequential compilations and five paired samples. It found no confirmed regression under the existing 30%/500 ns rule. It still measured approximately 15–19% overhead for reversing maintenance, 10–14% for maintained mobile frames, and 3–8% for ordinary stable-ID access. Those costs remain visible tradeoffs, not claims of zero regression. Linux evidence comes from the PR checks; actual GPU execution is validated separately and is not included in these CPU performance numbers.

data: These comparisons have distinct layouts and environments. The Linux report compares growable stores with 256-row-capped blocks; the macOS report compares historical bounded blocks with row reordering. Keep those controls separate. The growable results were recorded in documentation commit 6d7c2ea; its text does not identify an exact current implementation SHA beyond decision 0014. The macOS comparison does identify its implementation and base revisions. Below, “current” refers to the candidate in each comparison.
data.partitioned-storage-comparison#Partition:
Build the optimized standalone driver once: pixi run mojo build -I src benchmark/partitioned_spatial.mojo -o /tmp/larecs-partition-benchmark. Run that binary without concurrent compilation or benchmark jobs. Partitioning is explicitly selected at registration; the control is the same current library’s deferred row reordering, not forced full classification or a historical library with different invalidation costs. The existing core/spatial PR gate separately measures changes to the default paths against the exact base.
The driver constructs identical deterministic scrambled 2,048/32,768-row worlds with two component-defined archetypes, 64-byte SIMD payloads, an integer input, and an additional eight-byte column on half the rows. It compares one growable store per logical cluster with row reordering for uniform (16 identities per cell), dense (1,024 per cell), and singleton sparse (one identity per cell, key spacing 128) distributions. Each configuration warms both layouts with one sixteen-frame batch, then alternates their order for five paired sixteen-frame samples.
The 48 scenarios cover maintenance with 1, 1/64, or all identities updated; ordinary read-only query scans and host execution with unchanged layouts; and complete cell frames with the same updates, maintenance every frame (or every fourth frame for 1/64 updates), all-lane per-cell aggregation, and cyclic adjacent-cell aggregate products. Both layouts use identical entities, input updates, and semantic work. The scan controls still call the clean boundary. All measured update frames include marking, pending key allocation/copy, classification, directory construction or sorting, column growth/movement, source swap-removal, location repair, and allocation reclamation as applicable. Cell frames also include query setup, cell scratch allocation, aggregation, and neighbor arithmetic. Construction, initial placement, policy/device setup, and validation are excluded. There are no device transfers in these CPU timings.
Every sample checks all identities once, final inputs, all payload lanes, entity locations, default key order or homogeneous cluster stores, and equal complete spatial checksums outside timing. Query/host scan reductions are also checked against their complete expected sums. Results are consumed inside the timer. This is a synthetic spatial workload, not a game/simulation speedup, collision detection, or a persistent neighbor index.
MEMORY records report initial maintained capacity-derived owned bytes; MEMORY_AFTER_MOVEMENT reports retained buffers after 96 fully moving frames: physical-directory slots, component/ID buffers, entity locations, key/dirty caches, queued identities, and recycled-slot capacity. Counted allocations are physical-directory plus row-column/ID allocations. Graph/pool allocations, allocator overhead, device state, classifier configuration, and all temporary maintenance/query/cell scratch are excluded; these records are not RSS or peak memory measurements. The components are trivial and have no hidden payload heap. Columns in a store share capacity, but each column and the IDs allocate separately. PAIR records give rows, distribution, mode, update count, cadence, pair index, reordering ns/frame, and partition ns/frame.
Growable-store comparison on Linux The same current driver was built against committed base df0e6c5638beaab2bf3784a2b4784044a7c2707e (256-row-capped blocks) and the growable-store implementation from decision 0014. This local run used AMD Ryzen 7 PRO 5850U, Linux 7.2.5-3-omarchy x86_64, Mojo 1.0.0 (ed45d567), normal optimized builds without tracing, sanitizers, or debug information. Cold builds ran sequentially and took 11.13 s / 11.11 s (base/current). No other builds or benchmark jobs ran during timing; background desktop services remained active. Five pairs of fresh binary invocations alternated base/current order. Each invocation used the warmup, five paired sixteen-frame samples per case, timing boundaries, and complete validation described above. Values below are medians of the five per-invocation medians, in milliseconds. All 48 cases validated in all ten invocations. Median complete driver execution including validation was 13.10 s / 11.33 s (base/current).
Driver SHA-256: 37795c49baa95f1b911d43327d413097b85a5f60f92f3137accf7abfa9a90ad9.
Distribution Timed work, 32,768 rows Capped blocks Growable stores Growable / capped Uniform Maintenance, 512 updates/frame 0.416 0.256 0.61 Dense Maintenance, 512 updates/frame 0.111 0.072 0.65 Dense Complete frame, all moving 6.032 4.295 0.71 Singleton sparse Complete frame, all moving 20.400 17.231 0.84 Dense Ordinary query scan, clean 0.430 0.427 0.99 Dense Ordinary CPU scan, clean 0.030 0.031 1.03 Uniform Ordinary CPU scan, clean 0.068 0.070 1.03 Singleton sparse Ordinary CPU scan, clean 0.337 0.344 1.02 Dense initial placement used 64 stores and 225 counted allocations, versus 128 blocks and 449 allocations in the base. Initial counted owned bytes fell from 4,448,265 to 4,403,209. After 96 fully moving frames, growable dense stores retained 7,847,945 bytes and 64,512 row slots, versus 5,062,665 bytes and 32,768 slots for capped blocks. Destination stores can grow while their old rows are still awaiting transfer, and nonempty stores retain that spare capacity. Fewer stores therefore do not guarantee less retained memory. These remain capacity-derived buffer measurements, with the exclusions described above.
Full scans changed by -0.8% to +4.3% across these distributions; small timing differences on this desktop runner do not establish a scan improvement. Maintenance and fully moving frame results favor growable stores here, but singleton clusters still have separate allocations and substantial traversal overhead. This is CPU-only synthetic evidence; macOS, GPU, application, peak memory, and additional component-width comparisons remain on the roadmap. Local raw reports are retained under output/performance/growable_clusters/.
Historical bounded-block comparison on macOS The measurements below are historical evidence for decision 0013’s 256-row-capped blocks, not timings for the current growable-store layout. Dense clusters now use fewer stores; sparse clusters still require separate allocations. Rerun the driver before making performance claims about the new layout.
A local optimized run on Apple M4, macOS 27.0.1 arm64, Mojo 1.0.0 (ed45d567), implementation f3d99cd (base 6037850), built in 7.59 seconds and completed execution/validation in 8.88 seconds. After 96 fully moving frames, counted retained bytes were 4,883,849 for reordering versus 10,116,809 uniform, 5,062,665 dense, and 51,019,785 singleton partitions at 32,768 rows. Small dense/uniform updates took less elapsed maintenance time with partitions, while directory rebuilding and per-block scans dominated singleton cases. The benchmark measures total elapsed costs, not byte-movement counters. Fully moving workloads were slower despite local transfer. Keep partitions opt-in, and retain the reordering default. The measured bounded-block implementation copied identity-capacity keys, inspected blocks, and could move unchanged rows during same-cluster compaction. The current layout retains key copying and directory scans but removes cross-block compaction; destination growth can still relocate existing columns. Cluster selection scans metadata. Application workloads, other component widths, structural-heavy frames, Linux comparative timings, process/peak memory, and device timings remain on the roadmap. GPU functional integration ran on the actual local accelerator; it is separate evidence from these CPU performance measurements.
The separate default-path PR gate against 6037850 passed all twelve core and 32 spatial cases in 49.2 seconds, including four sequential builds and five paired samples. It required no regression confirmation. Ordinary 2,048-row query/host execution changes were +0.1%/-0.6%, stable-ID access was +3.9%, and selected mutation was +0.9% in that run. These small shared-machine differences are not a zero-overhead guarantee; the existing 30%/500 ns rule is unchanged. Hosted Linux/macOS evidence is retained by the PR checks.

data: These are recorded execution budgets for an unchanged-library comparison, not platform speed rankings. The hosted record identifies merge checkout ba8b180; the earlier local record identifies baseline 688fb67 but not its exact current checkout SHA. Hardware/compiler, method, excluded costs, and confirmation limits are preserved below. Current commands and failure rules live in regression operation.
data.initial-gate-measurements#Initial gate m:
The initial unchanged-library comparison against 688fb67 on Apple M4, macOS 27 arm64, Mojo 1.0.0 (ed45d567), took 55.3 seconds: core builds 9.3/9.6 seconds and sampling 2.6 seconds; spatial builds 5.8/5.4 seconds and sampling 22.2 seconds. Builds and samples ran sequentially; no concurrent builds or benchmark jobs ran. These are driver compilation costs in an already installed environment, not dependency installation time.
The first hosted run compared the same unchanged library against 688fb67, using PR merge checkout ba8b180, Mojo 1.0.0 (ed45d567), the same current driver on each side, fresh output binaries, sequential compilation/sampling, and five alternating pairs. Both suites passed without confirmation, and both artifact uploads succeeded:
Runner CPU / OS All driver builds All sampling Total gate macos-latest Apple M2 Pro (Virtual), macOS 26.6.2 arm64 43.1 s 22.1 s 66.1 s ubuntu-latest AMD EPYC 7763, Linux 6.17 x86_64 / glibc 2.39 50.2 s 24.6 s 75.3 s These are one-run runtime measurements, not speed comparisons between platforms or evidence that the runner’s load is stable. Full correctness tests, examples, package checks, and environment installation are excluded from these gate costs. The combined check stays near a minute; further coverage requires new budget measurements on both platforms. Confirmation adds sampling cost for affected suites; command deadlines bound failures rather than promising a one-minute runtime for all error/confirmation paths.

data: This report records Apple M4/macOS 27.0.1 results with Mojo 1.0.0 (ed45d567), base 6a3841b, and the portable-adapter work recorded in fde2cb9. The original text did not identify the exact measured current-tree SHA; fde2cb9 identifies the retained report/driver, not proof of a clean timed tree. The measured read-only adapter implementation predates later mutable-adapter and device-copy-reuse work. Its transfer costs are not current API guarantees. Below, “current” means that measured candidate rather than today’s checkout.
data.resource-execution#Resource execution:
resource_execution_benchmark.mojo uses the current execution API. Compare the same workload against the base library, adapting only backend call spelling when the base predates ExecutionBackend. It measures complete calls over 512 Int32 rows with either no resources or one legacy scalar resource. resource_adapter_benchmark.mojo measures current read-only adapters over the same rows and 4,096 initial Int32 samples. Only the first sample is read; the entire source is uploaded. Each timed adapter call edits that sample, and growth cases append one sample per call. Host calls use 10,000 iterations; GPU calls use 100. One warmup invocation precedes each timer. Construction and final checks are excluded; validation, leases, component transfers, resource uploads/downloads, allocation growth, and synchronization are included when applicable. Exact outputs, row counts, source values, and final sample lengths are checked outside timing.
Copy the current driver for the baseline build:
cp benchmark/resource_execution_benchmark.mojo /tmp/resource_base.mojo If the base accepts on_device: Bool rather than backend: ExecutionBackend, adapt only that copy before compiling it:
python - <<'PYCODE' from pathlib import Path import re path = Path("/tmp/resource_base.mojo") source = path.read_text().replace(" ExecutionBackend,\n", "") source, count = re.subn( r"backend=\(\s*ExecutionBackend\.DEVICE if device else ExecutionBackend\.HOST\s*\)", "on_device=device", source, ) assert count == 4, "Review the driver before adapting a changed call matrix" assert "ExecutionBackend" not in source.split('from std.time', 1)[1] path.write_text(source) PYCODE This maps the same compile-time device boolean to the older keyword; kernels, row counts, iterations, warmup, validation, and timing boundaries stay identical. Do not substitute a historical driver with different workloads. Device comparisons require a working accelerator on both sides; an older host fallback is not a device measurement. For a base using on_gpu, use that keyword instead.
Build optimized binaries once without debug information, sanitizers, or tracing:
pixi run mojo build -I /path/to/base/src /tmp/resource_base.mojo -o /tmp/resource-base pixi run mojo build -I src benchmark/resource_execution_benchmark.mojo -o /tmp/resource-current pixi run mojo build -I src benchmark/resource_adapter_benchmark.mojo -o /tmp/resource-adapters On Apple M4, macOS 27.0.1, Mojo 1.0.0 (ed45d567), compare base 6a3841b against this implementation with the same driver. Warm each binary, then run five paired samples, alternating base/current order, with no concurrent compilation or benchmark jobs. Median per-call means were:
Complete invocation Base Current Host, no resource 294.2 ns 299.6 ns Host, legacy scalar resource 299.8 ns 350.7 ns GPU, no resource 250.50 µs 251.52 µs GPU, legacy scalar resource 243.51 µs 268.59 µs Host, edited adapter — 449.1 ns Host, edited adapter plus growth — 451.4 ns GPU, edited adapter — 323.76 µs GPU, edited adapter plus growth — 303.54 µs The scalar GPU case costs about 10.3% more with staged publication and lifetime protection. These measurements establish the cost of this synthetic workload, not an application speedup or Tree-D shading result. Short GPU batches are noisy; the growth-case ordering does not establish a growth benefit. Source/sample allocation and scientific preprocessing during initial construction are excluded; incremental host append and device allocation growth are included in growth cases. Existing allocation capacity is reused in nongrowing cases; contents are uploaded every run.
Sequential base/current/adapter driver builds took 1.18/3.00/3.01 seconds with existing compiler caches and no competing builds. These are recorded build costs, not comparable cold-compilation measurements. Linux resource timings and cold compilation remain unmeasured. These focused manual cases do not enlarge the normal PR performance matrix.

data.early-selection-sample#Early selection s:
The following sample was recorded in documentation commit 1f44b03. Its exact measured implementation revision, compiler build, OS version, and accelerator model were not recorded. Its driver/workload are identified, but the sample cannot support a reproducible cross-version comparison.
The focused entity_selection_benchmark.mojo workload compares ordinary full-world host execution with contiguous and disjoint 64-row selections in a 100,000-row world, a selected add/remove chain, and selected device execution when an accelerator is available. On the Apple Metal development host used for the 1.0.0b2 work, one bounded run measured approximately 0.0253 ms for the 100k-row host path, 0.0000664 ms for the contiguous selection, 0.000556 ms for 64 disjoint single-row ranges, 0.00727 ms for the add/remove chain, and 0.379 ms for the device selection. These are development measurements, not a cross-version historical baseline; use the benchmark on target hardware for regression decisions.
The manual host thread dispatch experiment compares complete sequential kernel calls with dynamically claimed whole-store and contiguous chunk jobs at 1/2/4 worker tasks, including small and large increment/compute workloads and single-store cases. Its driver, timing boundaries, reproduction commands, and Linux measurements are recorded there. It is a restricted feasibility benchmark; the current experimental engine adds eligibility and lifecycle checks absent from that prototype. Both drivers remain outside the normal PR performance gate.
data.shared-host-execution-comparison#Shared:
The focused selection driver also measures thin and lexical host kernels over seven matching archetypes (512 rows each) alongside six nonmatching archetypes (512 rows each). All matching rows perform the same increment; the closure also counts range invocations. Construction and result checks are excluded, and checks outside the timer verify row count, every row against Bencher.num_iters, and the closure’s exact invocation count and accumulated values. These cases remain manual benchmarks; they are not added to the small PR suite.
On Apple M4, macOS 27.0.1, Mojo 1.0.0 (ed45d567), the shared host setup refactor in 1cd32ba was compared with 688fb670c87ced6b08c920e2c3527a1890218c6f using the same updated driver and compiler environment. Build one optimized binary against an isolated baseline checkout and one against the current source, without -g, sanitizers, or tracing. Warm each once, then alternate baseline/current order across five paired samples with no concurrent builds or benchmark jobs. The driver uses fixed iterations: 100 full-world calls, 1,000 multi-archetype calls, 10,000 contiguous selected calls, and 1,000 disjoint selected calls.
Host workload Baseline median Refactor median 100,000 rows, full-world thin 23.33 µs 22.89 µs 3,584 rows, seven matching archetypes, thin 1.269 µs 1.034 µs Same rows, lexical closure 1.089 µs 0.885 µs 64 selected contiguous rows in a 100k world 69.0 ns 18.5 ns 64 selected disjoint single-row ranges in a 100k world 690 ns 257 ns The unchanged mutation controls measured 10.13 → 10.09 µs for a 64-row add/remove chain and 107 → 98 µs for the first 512-row disjoint mutation pass. The existing selected device case ran on the actual Apple M4 accelerator and measured 276.31 → 267.52 µs.
