data: This record preserves the standalone driver protocol. No hardware, compiler, run revision, or timing results were recorded with this section, so it makes no measured performance claim. The driver is available at the documentation revision through its source. Current implementation details are in synchronization internals.
data.synchronization-primitives#Synchronizati:
benchmark/synchronization_benchmark.mojo is a focused manual comparison of 100,000 sequential scalar increments using a plain scalar control, direct Mojo relaxed atomics, Larecs relaxed atomic views, and uncontended write guards. Every case performs equivalent increments and consumes results. Setup and final exact total validation are excluded; guard acquisition, payload access, and release are included. These are isolated uncontended costs, not complete ECS execution, contention, allocation, transfer, or GPU measurements. No new timing cases are added to the normal PR performance suite.
Build once without debug information, sanitizers, or tracing, warm the binary, then run repeated samples without other builds or benchmark jobs:
pixi run mojo build -I src benchmark/synchronization_benchmark.mojo -o /tmp/larecs-synchronization /tmp/larecs-synchronization Report compilation time separately from execution and retain hardware/compiler details with timing claims. Concurrent compound access and exact atomic totals are correctness checks in test/synchronization_test.mojo; contended performance and complete binding/transfer measurements remain roadmap work.

data: The measurements below concern the implemented engine at 4489ceb, on AMD Ryzen 7 PRO 5850U, Linux x86-64, Mojo 1.0.0 (ed45d567), MAX 26.5.0. The host-dispatch feasibility investigation retains a different prototype and must not substitute for this engine.
data.threaded-host-execution#Threaded host ex:
benchmark/threaded_execution.mojo measures the implemented public SystemContext.run[kernel, threaded=True]() against unchanged sequential calls. Both worlds have identical initial rows, arithmetic, and layout. The driver covers 1/2/4 worker tasks, one/four stores, balanced and seven-to-one skewed stores, 1,024–1,048,576 total rows, and increments or 32 dependent arithmetic rounds per row. It forces min_parallel_rows=0 to expose dispatch overhead; configured one-worker runs still use whole-range sequential fallback.
Each case warms both paths twice, calibrates the sequential path to a 10 ms batch or at most 4,096 calls, then alternates order across five paired samples. Complete-call timing includes discovery, validation, spatial-invalidation checks, resource binding, context allocation, atomic claiming, dispatch, join, cleanup, and world-size consumption. Construction, initial runtime warmup, compilation, and exact result validation are excluded. Every final row is validated against all warmup, calibration, and measured calls. No resources or spatial classifiers are bound; shared-resource, selected, and partitioned correctness lives in the tests, while their performance remains unmeasured here.
pixi run mojo build -I src benchmark/threaded_execution.mojo -o /tmp/larecs-threaded-benchmark /tmp/larecs-threaded-benchmark /tmp/larecs-threaded-benchmark /tmp/larecs-threaded-benchmark Build once without debug info, tracing, or sanitizers. Run measurements without other builds or benchmark jobs. Each PAIR line contains skew flag, base rows per store, store count, arithmetic rounds, worker count, pair index, calls per batch, sequential ns/call, and threaded ns/call. In skewed cases, total rows are ten times the base row count. Report compilation separately and retain hardware/compiler details; this synthetic comparison establishes no portable cutoff, fixed speedup, or application-level benefit.
At revision 4489ceb, on Linux x86-64 (7.2.5-3-omarchy), AMD Ryzen 7 PRO 5850U (8 cores, 16 hardware threads), Mojo 1.0.0 (ed45d567), and MAX 26.5.0, the optimized build took 17.57 seconds in the installed environment; this is not a cold-cache compilation measurement. Three serial binary runs took 7.12, 7.48, and 7.70 seconds after regression builds completed. All 30 scenarios and 450 paired measurements passed exact result validation. Raw local output is retained in ignored output/threaded-execution/run-{1,2,3}.txt files.
Four-worker results below summarize 15 pairs per case. Times are medians in microseconds per complete call; speedup is the median paired ratio, so it need not equal the ratio of the displayed medians.

data: Use a repository checkout to build Larecs and check a change against its locked toolchain. The supported Pixi platforms are Linux x86-64 and macOS Apple Silicon. Application installation has a separate guide.
data.build-a-package#Build a package:
Precompile the source package, then build an example against that package:
pixi run mojo precompile src/larecs -o /tmp/larecs.mojoc pixi run mojo build -I /tmp examples/particles/movement.mojo -o /tmp/larecs-movement /tmp/larecs-movement This checks package consumption without -I src. The final program must produce the same result as the source smoke run. CI also performs a package smoke check; generated packages are disposable build outputs.
data.install-and-smoke-test#Install and smoke:
From the repository root, install the locked environments and run the checked movement program:
pixi install --locked pixi run mojo --version pixi run mojo run -I src examples/particles/movement.mojo The program prints All particles reached their expected positions. after asserting the results. The root manifest declares Mojo >=1.0.0,<1.1.0, MAX >=26.5.0,<27, and mojo-tracy >=1.1.0,<2; pixi.lock pins the actual resolution. Retain the reported compiler build with verification evidence. The separate scripts environment pins documentation tools.
data.resolve-platform-failures#Resolve platfo: Symptom Action Metal compiler crashes compiling a GPU iterator with -g Add # SKIP_DEBUG to every GPU-launching test. Keep the actual GPU path; see the Metal compiler workaround. libSystem.tbd reports unknown arm64e.x1 architecture Install an older compatible macOS SDK and leave SDKROOT unset so Pixi activation can choose it. An explicit SDKROOT is respected; see the SDK workaround. A focused test needs a custom invocation pixi run tests --no-precompile test/<filename>.mojo omits package precompilation; keep include/linker settings consistent with the wrapper. The canonical coding standards and test wrapper remain at their repository paths. Build documentation when examples or contracts change.
data.run-focused-checks-then-the-suite#Run fo:
For a storage-lifecycle change, run the focused test before the full suite:
pixi run tests test/host_storage_lifecycle_test.mojo pixi run tests test pixi run test-resource-compile-failures The test wrapper precompiles Larecs and uses assertions, debug information, tracing linkage, and AddressSanitizer unless a file opts out. A full directory run also executes compile-contract checks and bounded core/spatial performance checks. Focused files trigger their associated contracts but omit performance checks. The resource compile-failure fixture task is a separate CI step. Use test and hardware coverage to select the right checks and interpret device skips. Optimized performance measurements need separate untraced, unsanitized binaries.

data:
Mojo package · Source
Use the curated reference to choose an API and look up compatibility. This module tree contains the full compiler-generated declarations, including implementation utilities.
Larecs🌲 is a performance-oriented archetype-based ECS for Mojo.
It is based on the ECS Arche, implemented in the Go programming language.
Larecs 1.0 is currently in beta, so public APIs may still change before the stable 1.0.0 release. After that release, public APIs follow semantic versioning unless they are explicitly marked experimental. Device execution is currently such an experimental API. Threaded host execution is also experimental.
Build the particle simulation for a complete program using systems and kernels. You can find its source in examples/particles/movement.mojo.

Mojo module · Source
Component type registration and validation.
Provides ComponentManager, which assigns compile-time IDs to component types and offers helpers for checking their validity.
data.aliases#Aliases:
ComponentType The trait that components must conform to.
ComponentType = Copyable & Deinitable DeviceComponentType Trait subset of ComponentType safe for device raw-byte transfer.
DeviceComponentType = TrivialRegisterPassable SystemContext.run(..., backend=ExecutionBackend.DEVICE) moves component columns between host and device buffers via a plain byte copy (see DeviceComponentStorage): the destination never runs T’s copy constructor or destructor, only memcpys its bytes. That is only sound for a type with no non-trivial state – no owned heap allocation, no custom copy/move/destroy logic – since a bitwise copy of such a type would corrupt or leak it. TrivialRegisterPassable already encodes exactly that constraint at the type-system level (bitwise copyable, trivially destroyed, and transitively so for every member), so it is reused here rather than inventing a new marker trait.
It also already implies Copyable & Deinitable (i.e. ComponentType), so it alone is the constraint – composing it with ComponentType would be redundant.

@memory_only struct HostStorage[*ComponentTypes: ComponentType] Holds all the component and entity data for a world.
This is always used in combination with a World instance, e.g. as a member of it.
Access it through world.storage, for example var entity = world.storage.add_entity(Position(10.0, 20.0)). Change one entity’s components shows a complete program.

query Returns a locked, read-only iterator over all Entities matching the filter.
def query[filter: Filter](mut self, out iterator: LockedEntityRange[origin_of(self._archetypes), origin_of(self._locks), ComponentTypes, row_filter=iterator.filter]) Exact declaration def query[filter: Filter[iterator.filter._include, iterator.filter._exclude, iterator.filter._is_exclusive, iterator.filter._read, iterator.filter._written]](mut self, out iterator: LockedEntityRange[origin_of(self._archetypes), origin_of(self._locks), ComponentTypes, row_filter=iterator.filter]) The lock is acquired immediately and held for the iterator’s lifetime, preventing structural changes to the world until it is dropped. The iterator can be copied; every copy preserves the current traversal position and acquires a distinct lock that is released independently. Copying aborts if no lock is available. Component values are read-only through this iterator; mutate components from inside a system instead, via SystemContext.run.
The yielded ArchetypeRowAccessor’s get[T]() is checked at compile time against filter: T must be included by filter (via Filter.include), since only then is every matching archetype guaranteed to carry it. Use unsafe_get[T]() for a component filter doesn’t guarantee, or has[T]() to check first.

@memory_only struct EntityAccessorIterator[filter: Filter[filter._include, filter._exclude, filter._is_exclusive, filter._read, filter._written]] Iterates filtered component rows with host or device-appropriate strides.
The iterator does not enumerate entity IDs or archetypes. It walks the dense rows described by KernelContext and yields an EntityAccessor containing a row offset and one byte-addressed pointer per included component. The accessor’s get and set methods use the filter’s compile-time component order to select a column, then use the row offset to access that column’s structure-of-arrays (SoA) element.
On the host, iteration starts at row 0 and advances by 1. The context therefore describes one homogeneous component range, normally a single matching archetype. On a device, is_gpu() removes the host path at compile time: each thread starts at global_idx.x and advances by the total number of threads in the launch. This gives every thread the rows global_idx.x, global_idx.x + thread_count, and so on, while the bounds check stops at context.length.
The same kernel source is consequently valid on both targets. Host contexts contain host pointers, while the device-passable host context is converted to device pointers before a device launch. The iterator itself performs no host/device copy or synchronization; callers must ensure the columns are initialized, have at least context.length rows, and that each row is written by at most one concurrent thread.

Returned by queries and low-level batch mutations. Query access is read-only; mutation results permit mutable setup access. System logic uses EntitySelection.run instead. Explicit range metadata and query archetype indices are immutable and shared across cursor copies.
Acquires the lock before initializing traversal and releases it on destruction, including early loop exits. Moving the wrapper transfers ownership of the lock without acquiring another one. @memory_only struct EntityPool EntityPool is an implementation using implicit linked lists.
Follows the entity recycling scheme from ECS back and forth, part 3.
Per-ID generations survive reset. Recycling or resetting advances the affected generations modulo 232; an ancient handle can alias a new one after 232 advances of its ID. Handles are local to a pool, and copying a pool creates an independent snapshot with the same handles and history. Copying takes O(high-water mark) time and storage, including retained IDs.

Stateless operations over the current source; no factory or adapter instance.
View[False] is the read view and View[True] the mutable view; they may be distinct types. Descriptors are immutable trivial values: mutable views reach shared state through pointers into adapter-managed backing buffers.
Views and their pointers must not escape a synchronous invocation. Every read view must support concurrent reads on its execution target, including view methods and all reachable data, without hidden unsafe mutation. No alias may mutate, resize, relocate, or free backing data before completion. The adapter author guarantees this; descriptor checks cannot prove it. Device preparation must transfer through ResourceDeviceCache, never enqueue a copy from an external host pointer. Validation must neither mutate nor queue work.
Mutable access is opt-in. supports_mutation admits write and read_write declarations on sequential host execution. GPU and threaded host execution additionally require supports_concurrent_mutation, which the author may declare only if every mutable view operation is safe under concurrent use, for example through atomics or provably disjoint writes. Larecs’s exclusive source lease does not prevent races among kernel workers; the user is responsible for safe resource access.

context.run[move](): run on the host, sequentially. context.run[move, threaded=True](): run on the host in concurrent chunks (experimental). context.run[move, backend=ExecutionBackend.DEVICE](): run on an accelerator (experimental). context.run[move](read_capture(x), mut_capture(y)): pass host-local values to a kernel that declares captures. filter, required_resources, and capture_spec are inferred from the kernel’s KernelContext parameter. The tutorial Your first simulation shows a complete program.
Execution: The call returns after all kernel work has finished.
Host: KernelFunc is called once per non-empty physical store matching filter, one store after the other. Each KernelContext iterates that store’s rows; row indices are local to the context. Threaded host: each matching store is split into chunks, and chunks may run concurrently on the world’s ThreadedExecutionConfig. With one worker or fewer matching rows than min_parallel_rows, the stores run sequentially. Device: one launch covers all matching rows. Readable columns and resources are uploaded when the device copy is not current; write-only columns are not uploaded, so the kernel must set them for every row. Written columns, read-write resources, and mutable captures are copied back before run returns. DEVICE never falls back to HOST. Access: include grants read-write component access, read read-only, and write set-only access; required_resources declares resource access the same way. Undeclared components and resources are rejected at compile time.
Empty matches: no kernel call happens. With DEVICE, the device storage and required resources are still validated, in that order, and a missing accelerator still raises.

def reuse_device_copies(mut self, enabled: Bool) Off by default. Larecs tracks revisions that conservatively advance on each Larecs access that may mutate data:
Resources: add, set, get through mutable storage, host runs declaring write or read_write, and device runs writing the resource. Component columns, per type and store: storage.get, set, apply, kernel runs writing the type, and every structural change, spatial reordering, or partition move of the store. With reuse enabled, a device run skips uploading a resource or a column segment whose device copy matches its current revision. Use world.resources.read[T]() and world.storage.read[T](entity) for reads between device runs, since mutable get counts as a mutation.
Mutations through references obtained before a later Larecs call, or through raw pointers, are not detected. Re-obtain references after a run, or call world.resources.invalidate_device[T]() or invalidate_device_copies() after such a mutation; otherwise the next device run reads stale values.

Use root imports such as from larecs import World, Filter, SystemContext for application code. The root export list in the generated package index is checked against the initializer’s actual imports during every build. Module-qualified names remain available in the generated module tree.
Surface Intended use Application APIs World, Entity, Filter, Scheduler, System, SystemContext, KernelContext, EntitySelection, Resources and the optional APIs linked above Supported lower-level APIs HostStorage, row accessors, EntityRange, ResourceStorage, component/resource traits and documented direct storage operations Implementation utilities Store allocation, component managers, device storage, lock managers, pools and transfer caches; these explain implementation mechanisms and are not the recommended application workflow Classification does not remove existing imports or compatibility commitments. data: This reference describes the development checkout, currently Larecs 1.0 beta. Public APIs may change before stable 1.0.0. After stable release, public APIs follow semantic versioning unless explicitly experimental. Threaded host and device execution, mutable resource adapters, and device-copy reuse are experimental.
data.cross-cutting-limits#Cross-cutting limit:
No device fallback backend=ExecutionBackend.DEVICE never falls back to host execution. Without accelerator support, or when the world’s device context failed to initialize, run raises, even when no rows match. Once a device run starts, initialization, transfer, and execution errors propagate to the caller. To use the host when no device is available, branch explicitly, for example on has_accelerator(), and call the ExecutionBackend.HOST specialization.
Empty queries and selections hold structural locks A live query, storage batch range, or entity selection holds a structural lock even when it matched nothing or its cursor is exhausted. While any lock is held, entity creation and deletion, component additions and removals, spatial maintenance, and cluster selection raise a locked-world error. The exception is a selection’s own add, remove, and replace, which work while that selection holds the world’s only lock; see EntitySelection. End the lock first: consume the query with ^, let it go out of scope, or close the selection’s with block.
Row indices are not entity IDs A kernel row’s idx counts from zero within one kernel invocation: one physical store, one selected range, or one threaded chunk. On a device, it is the row’s offset in the packed rows of one launch. The same entity can have a different idx in the next call, because structural changes, spatial maintenance, chunking, and packing all change it. Identify entities with Entity handles, and do not index shared output with idx.
Structural locks are not mutexes A structural lock keeps rows in place while a query, selection, or kernel uses them. A resource lease keeps a resource source alive and in place during a kernel call. Neither serializes threads, makes concurrent writes race-free, or protects against aliases obtained before the call, such as a pointer kept from an earlier get. Shared writes need per-row output, a single writer, or a synchronization primitive.
data.target-support#Target support:
Contract Sequential host Threaded host Device Thin kernel Supported; default threaded=True backend=ExecutionBackend.DEVICE Value-taking callable Supported, including lexical captures Rejected at compile time Rejected at compile time Components Host ComponentType, including nontrivial ownership Pointer-free trivial plain values TrivialRegisterPassable transfer check Ordinary resources Host resource traits; declared access Explicit read-only pointer-free plain values Recursively checked pointer-free plain values Portable resources Access-selected host views Mutable views require concurrent-mutation support Access-selected device views and adapter-managed transfers Explicit captures Read-only and mutable slots Unsupported Device-safe values and synchronous copy-back Scheduling One invocation per nonempty matching store Concurrent chunks; sequential below threshold or with one worker One launch across matching rows Completion Synchronous Synchronous Synchronous, including written data copied back A thin kernel is a named def function, such as move, that run receives as a compile-time parameter (context.run[move]()); it captures no local variables. Eligibility checks run independently of threaded worker count and fallback thresholds. Setting one worker does not allow nontrivial components, mutable ordinary resources, or captures through the threaded path.
The defining contracts are SystemContext.run, component.constrain_device_safe_components, resource.constrain_device_safe_resources, and DevicePassableResource. Portable resource sources control their view and transfer lifecycle; a component’s device eligibility does not establish a resource’s eligibility.
By default, readable device data uploads on every call. With world.reuse_device_copies(True), it uploads only when the cached copy is stale. Write-only columns skip upload and must be fully written. Read-only reuse therefore depends on revision tracking, not merely on calling the same kernel again. Device-copy reuse never skips written output copy-back.
Standalone atomic and guard primitives exist, with Apple device restrictions. Automatic kernel synchronization bindings and deferred retries are unimplemented.

Read each generated operation’s Raises and Constraints before handling a failure. Constraints reject invalid programs at compile time; runtime errors report invalid state or execution failures.
API or condition Meaning and response LarecsError Variant containing typed ECS errors and general Error failures. Inspect the specific error rather than assuming every failure is an invalid entity. EntityError, ComponentError Invalid or stale entity, or wrong component membership. Recheck the handle generation and requested composition. WorldError Includes structural lock exhaustion, a locked world and negative batch counts. Release queries and selections before structural changes, even empty ones; pass a nonnegative count. Device setup or synchronization failure run raises; there is no host fallback. Fix device availability or explicitly select HOST. See device failure behavior. Invalid resource or capture access Check declarations, presence, access modes and binding order. Synchronization cannot repair a declaration mismatch. Threaded resources require explicit read access (compile error) Ordinary threaded resources must declare read; mutable adapters need concurrent-mutation support. See threaded failures. Cluster selection requires clean spatial maintenance Release live selections and queries and maintain explicitly before selecting the next cluster. See spatial failures. Device reads stale data with reuse enabled Reacquire mutable references after each run or invalidate after escaped writes. See copy-reuse failures. TryAccess.is_acquired() is false The guard attempt is Busy. Record required unfinished work for a later pass; there is no automatic retry. See shared-write alternatives. A failing kernel call is not a transaction: do not infer rollback of writes already performed. Scoped selections release locks on exit, including exceptional exit. Failure effects specific to an operation remain in its defining declaration.
data.migration-spellings#Migration spellings:
Older examples may use direct World entity operations or boolean execution-target flags. Current single-entity setup uses world.storage; scheduled application updates use SystemContext. Select targets with backend=ExecutionBackend.HOST or backend=ExecutionBackend.DEVICE. Consult SystemContext.run for the current overloads.
Resource adapters written for the read-only adapter API need three changes:
Replace comptime View = MyView with comptime View[mut: Bool] = MyView. Change bind_host and prepare_device to return Self.View[False]. Remove comptime KernelView = MyView from the source. KernelView remains an alias for View[False]. Adapters that do not opt into mutation keep their behavior; mutable declarations of them fail to compile with “DevicePassableResource mutable access requires Adapter.supports_mutation”.
The changelog records release changes. The development reference does not imply that an unreleased declaration exists in a previously installed package.

data:
SystemContext.run executes a kernel synchronously. For a complete thin kernel named move, use context.run[move](). The first simulation defines its filter, components, resource, system and scheduler.
Call form Behavior context.run[move]() Default sequential host execution; one kernel call per matching nonempty physical store. context.run[move, threaded=True]() Experimental host chunks; eligibility checks still apply when configuration selects sequential execution. context.run[move, backend=ExecutionBackend.DEVICE]() Experimental accelerator execution with no host fallback. context.run(kernel_func) Value-taking callable overload; lexical host captures are allowed, but the target must be sequential HOST. context.run[move](read_capture(x), mut_capture(y)) Thin kernel with explicitly declared capture slots; bindings must follow the declared order. The generated run entry keeps overload anchors, access constraints, preparation errors, and both readable and exact compiler declarations. Read the compatibility matrix before changing targets.
API Contract System Implement update; optionally implement initialize and finalize. Scheduler Owns the world and registered systems; run(steps) initializes, updates for the requested steps, and finalizes. Individual lifecycle methods are also available. KernelContext Borrows the current component and resource view; iterate it for row access. Row indices are not entity IDs. ExecutionBackend Compile-time HOST or DEVICE; HOST is the default. ThreadedExecutionConfig Worker count, chunks per worker, and minimum row threshold; configuration alone does not enable threading. See Execution for complete particle programs per target. Kernels cannot perform arbitrary structural changes while execution holds structural locks. Cross-cutting limits covers device fallback, locks of empty queries, row indices, and locks versus mutexes.
data.device-copy-reuse#Device-copy reuse:
World.reuse_device_copies lets a device call skip uploading a resource or component column whose device copy is current. Written outputs still download after every call.
Data Operations that advance its revision Resource add, set, get through mutable storage, and host, threaded, or device runs declaring writable access. Removal discards its records. Component type in a physical store Mutable storage or row access, setters, and kernels declaring writes, including on exact selected ranges. All columns of affected stores Structural changes, spatial row permutations, partition transfers, and store growth or replacement. Escaped references or raw pointers Not tracked. Call world.resources.invalidate_device[T]() for one resource or World.invalidate_device_copies for all copies. read, read-only queries, and read access in kernels preserve reusable copies. A mutable get advances the revision even when the caller only reads. A component copy is reused only for the same store incarnation, contiguous row range, packed offset, and revision. Alternating filters or selections can change packed offsets and cause uploads of unchanged values. Read-only portable resources still validate and lease their sources; a current copy skips prepare_device and reuses its view. Mutable adapters always prepare. Explicit captures upload on every call. Failed invocations invalidate the copies they touched. A world copy starts with independent host owners and empty device records. Disabling reuse discards records; completion stays synchronous. Invalidation does not permit mutation during a live invocation and does not make an invalid reference safe.
data.device-execution#Device execution:
backend=ExecutionBackend.DEVICE is a compile-time choice; a runtime choice needs an explicit branch calling each specialization. Device calls accept only thin kernels and visit each matched row once in one launch, using grid-stride iteration.
Topic Contract Availability Larecs checks device availability before resource preparation and has no host fallback. Components Only accessed component types are checked; each must be TrivialRegisterPassable. Ordinary resources Recursively checked pointer-free trivial values with read or read_write access; write is rejected. PlainValue is a trusted declaration for opaque pointer-free trivial fields, not permission to transfer pointers. Mutable shared values require race-free writes. Transfers By default every call uploads all readable columns and resources. Larecs packs only matching ranges and scatters written columns back to their original host stores; rows outside a selection stay untouched. Resource views and capture values bind separately from columns. Allocation capacity can persist between calls. Write-only components write[T]() permits set, not get. Previous host bytes are not uploaded, so the kernel must set every visited row. Empty match Required resources and adapters still validate; no device allocation, upload, or launch occurs. Captures stay unchanged. Mutable adapters still prepare and finalize host output. A missing resource raises. Completion run returns after the launch, synchronization, and copy-back of written components, read-write resources, and mutable captures. Downloads land in owned staging buffers and are published, that is written to their host destinations, only after successful synchronization. Failure A transfer or synchronization failure discards unpublished staged outputs and drains the queue. If completion stays unknown, the world rejects further execution and must be replaced. Host effects are not rolled back. An adapter finalizer can raise after publication; published outputs remain.
data.threaded-execution#Threaded execution:
threaded=True splits the rows of one call into kernel chunks; systems still run in registration order.
Topic Contract Kernel and target A nonraising thin kernel on ExecutionBackend.HOST. Lexical closures, explicit captures, and threaded=True with DEVICE fail at compile time. EntitySelection.run supports the same engine on exact selected ranges. Components Accessed components must be pointer-free trivial plain values. Unaccessed owning components can coexist in the world. A PlainValue declaration admits opaque scalar-only StaticTuple or InlineArray fields; its author guarantees the whole representation is pointer-free and trivial. Ordinary resources Explicit read access and a pointer-free plain value. Writable access, including the Resources[T]() read-write default, is rejected even when the configuration selects sequential execution. Portable resources Read views bind once on the coordinating caller and are shared until all workers join. Mutable views require supports_concurrent_mutation; the race-free write contract belongs to the adapter author. Configuration ThreadedExecutionConfig defaults to one worker, four chunks per worker, and a 65,536 matched-row cutoff. workers is a submitted-task budget, not reserved cores or guaranteed OS-thread overlap. Worker and chunk counts must be positive and their product representable; the cutoff must be nonnegative, and zero disables it. Sequential path With one worker, or fewer matched rows than the cutoff, calls keep whole-range sequential granularity after all eligibility checks. Empty matches invoke no kernel. Chunking Each physical store or selected range splits independently. Workers claim chunks dynamically in unspecified order. Code outside the row loop runs once per chunk, idx starts at zero in each chunk, and KernelContext.thread_count is one. Dependencies between chunks need a later run. Locks and preparation Every threaded call acquires one extra structural lock, including the sequential path and calls on an already locked selection. Lock exhaustion raises before work starts. All fallible preparation precedes row writes. Completion and failure All workers join before run returns. Fatal worker or runtime failures offer no rollback. Aliases Keep one coordinating caller per world. Do not reenter execution, mutate backing resources, or resize or relocate storage through escaped aliases while workers run. Copying, moving, replacing, or destroying an active world aborts. Avoid mutable globals and callees with hidden unsafe mutation.

data:
World owns the component storage and shared resource storage for a fixed compile-time component type pack. Use World[Position, Velocity]() during setup, then pass world^ to Scheduler to transfer ownership. The first simulation supplies the complete definitions and an asserted result.
API Contract and common form Entity A handle containing an ID and generation; retain handles rather than row addresses across structural changes. get_id() alone does not establish identity after recycling. HostStorage.is_alive world.storage.is_alive(entity) checks whether the generation still names a live entity. HostStorage.add_entity world.storage.add_entity(Position(0, 0), Velocity(1, 0)) creates an entity and returns its handle. HostStorage.get world.storage.get[Position](entity) borrows an existing component. Adding, removing or migrating entities can invalidate row references. HostStorage.set Replace an existing component value without changing the component set. HostStorage.replace world.storage.replace[Removed]().by(value, entity=entity) changes the component set. component.ComponentType Required component traits; host components can own nontrivial data. Heap ownership adds allocation and lifecycle costs. The generated type pages retain exact constructor declarations and overloads. The compatibility table distinguishes host component support from device transfer eligibility.

Filter combines membership and kernel permissions at compile time. The common form Filter().include[Position]().read[Velocity]() requires Position and Velocity, grants read-write access to Position, and grants read-only access to Velocity. include[Position] names a filter type and () constructs it; the shorter spelling Filter().include[Position].read[Velocity]() builds the same filter.
API Contract Filter.include, Filter.read, Filter.write Include component types with read-write, read-only or set-only access. A write-only kernel must initialize every selected output row. Filter.exclude, Filter.exclusive Exclude listed types, or match exactly the included composition. exclusive resets earlier exclusions; its generated declaration describes composition. HostStorage.query world.storage.query[filter]() creates a read-only query holding a structural lock. Release it before structural mutations. ArchetypeRowAccessor A borrowed row view; get_entity() returns a durable handle. Component references remain tied to the row and storage lifetime. EntityRange A physical store index, first row, and row count; it describes a bounded interval, not a list of handles. SystemContext.add_entities with context.add_entities(Position(0, 0), count=count) as selected: creates an exact scoped selection. Negative counts raise; zero creates an empty selection. EntitySelection.run Runs only the selection’s retained ranges. Exiting the scope releases its structural locks, including when the body raises. Queries inspect rows; kernels mutate components according to their filter. Selections restrict kernel work to the rows returned by the structural operation. See inspect entities outside a kernel for a complete example.

ResourceStorage stores one shared value per resource type. Add values during setup with world.resources.add(Time(0.25)). Declare a kernel’s access with Resources, for example Resources().read[Time](); undeclared access fails at compile time.
API Contract ResourceStorage.add, ResourceStorage.set, ResourceStorage.remove Insert, replace or remove a value; generated entries state presence requirements and failure behavior. Resources read grants immutable access, write fresh output access, and read_write mutable access preserving existing contents. DevicePassableResource Owning resource sources opt into adapter-built kernel views and become portable resources. The selected view depends on declared access and execution target. ResourceAdapter, ResourceAccess Adapter protocol and READ, WRITE, READ_WRITE modes; fresh WRITE does not preserve prior contents. BufferResource, ReadBuffer Buffer source and immutable view for portable resources. ResourceDeviceCache Allocation cache used by the adapter protocol; it does not replace a source’s ownership or revision contract. Captures, ReadCapture, MutCapture Ordered declarations for explicitly bound host-local values, independent of resource types. read_capture, mut_capture Bind borrowed values in declaration order; keep their owners alive through the synchronous call. Ordinary resources can own heap data on sequential host execution. Device plain resources require a recursively checked pointer-free representation; an owning resource instead needs an adapter. These rules differ from the component transfer check; see compatibility.
The portable resource guide and capture guide provide independent particle programs. Reuse unchanged device copies covers revisions and escaped-reference invalidation.
data.adapter-contracts#Adapter contracts:
A DevicePassableResource source names a stateless ResourceAdapter. Adapters register automatically when the source is added or inserted with set; there is no adapter factory. Kernels request the source type and receive its view; lookup uses source identity, so two sources may share a view type.
Hook or topic Contract validate Runs before binding either target on every call, including empty matches and current reused copies. bind_host Returns a view into the retained source, never into a temporary. Its untracked origin states the lifetime obligation; it does not transfer ownership. prepare_device Uploads through ResourceDeviceCache. cache.upload snapshots supported pointer-free trivial samples in owned staging buffers before enqueueing. Use distinct nonnegative stable slots per array; Larecs reserves slot -1 for the descriptor. Do not enqueue copies from external host pointers or temporary allocations. Cache Belongs to the source type, world, and device context. It retains allocation capacity; by default preparation still uploads current data on each call. Leases Larecs validates sources, leases them, and retains views until synchronous completion, including the join of threaded workers. Reentrant lookup, replacement, or removal of a leased source raises. Copying, moving, or destroying leased storage through an escaped alias aborts. View lifetime Views, their pointers, and references obtained from them must not escape the invocation. The pointer in a view is target-local. Read views Every read view and all reachable storage must support concurrent reads without hidden mutation. An immutable pointer field alone does not establish this. Escaped aliases must not mutate, resize, relocate, or free the backing collection while a call uses it. Threaded calls bind read adapters once on the coordinating caller.
data.explicit-captures#Explicit captures: Topic Contract Slots Captures lists slots in order. Bindings must match the slot count, types, and mutability in that order; slots may share a type. context.captures.get[i]() is immutable for a ReadCapture slot. Mutable slots One MutCapture value is shared by every invocation and every device thread, not private per row. Mutable access supplies no synchronization; use one proven writer or per-row output. Host binding Host execution borrows the original values until run returns. Device binding Device execution uploads every binding on each call and copies mutable slots back before run returns. Device captures copy trivial bytes and must own no heap data; there is no DevicePassableResource conversion. Empty match Captures stay unchanged. Targets Sequential host and device accept explicit captures; threaded execution rejects them at compile time. Lexical closures require sequential host execution. Lifetime References and pointers from capture slots or lexical borrows must not escape the invocation. Do not capture an alias that structurally changes the world while rows are borrowed.
data.mutable-adapters#Mutable adapters:
Mutable portable resources are experimental.
supports_mutation permits writable views on sequential host calls; supports_concurrent_mutation additionally permits them on threaded and device calls. Both are author guarantees: a source lease does not prevent races among the workers of one invocation, because leases are not mutexes. write selects fresh, adapter-initialized output; read_write preserves existing contents. The descriptor itself stays immutable; its methods control writes to backing storage. Preparation and finalization run once per invocation, even for empty matches. Mutable adapters prepare on every call, even with device-copy reuse. Resources[T]() without a mode means read-write and fails to compile for an adapter without supports_mutation. The checked scatter example shows the hooks and an atomic slot reservation.

data:
Spatial classification groups entities by application-defined keys. It changes physical placement without changing an entity’s component composition or identity; row indices are not entity IDs.
API Contract SpatialClassifier Define the classification key for the registered component types. grid_cell Convert position coordinates to a grid cell using the supplied cell size. morton_key_3d Encode a three-dimensional integer cell as a Morton key within the documented coordinate limits. AtomicValue, AtomicView Own an atomic value or borrow an atomic view; operations expose their memory ordering parameters. CompareExchangeResult Reports compare-exchange success and the observed value. Synchronized, SyncView Own guarded state or borrow its view. Use nonblocking try_read or try_write and check acquisition. TryAccess Test is_acquired() before consuming the result with take(). Keep access within the acquired guard’s lifetime. The generated declarations define supported value types, origins, mutation rights and memory orderings. See maintaining particle locality and coordinating shared writes for complete examples. Synchronization does not grant undeclared component/resource access or permit structural mutation during kernel execution.
data.classifier-registration#Classifier regis: world.register_spatial_classifier[filter](classifier, partitioned=...) stores one copyable classifier per world; a second registration raises, as does registration on a locked world. Registration requests a full rebuild but moves no rows. Only archetypes matching the registration filter participate. All filter types must belong to the world. The classifier’s Accessor must match the filter exactly; writable include or write inputs are rejected. Ordinary include, exclude, and exclusive rules apply. classify must be deterministic, must not mutate the world, and must not retain accessors or references. grid_cell floors coordinate / width. Coordinates and width must be finite, the width positive, and the resulting cell within [-1048576, 1048575]. morton_key_3d biases each signed 21-bit axis and interleaves the bits into a collision-free 63-bit key. Invalid inputs raise; they never clamp or wrap.
data.cluster-selection#Cluster selection: SystemContext.select_cluster returns an EntitySelection of the rows whose maintained key equals the requested key, across logical archetypes and intersected with the given filter. It raises without partition mode, without clean maintenance, or on a locked world. Membership stays fixed until release, even after member positions change. Even an empty selection holds a structural lock. Cluster selection scans store metadata; it is exact key equality, not a radius query, and Morton key adjacency does not imply spatial adjacency.
data.spatial-maintenance#Spatial maintenance:
World.maintain_spatial is the only operation that moves rows for classification. Kernel and system completion never run it.
Topic Contract Preconditions Raises on a locked world; see empty queries and selections hold structural locks. Component references do not survive maintenance, even a clean no-op; reacquire them by entity handle. Row ordering (partitioned=False) Sorts eligible rows by ascending key within their component-defined physical stores. Equal keys become contiguous; tie order is unspecified. Unchanged rows can move to restore contiguous groups. Partitions (partitioned=True) One growable dense store per logical archetype and cluster key. Capacity starts at one row and doubles; there is no fixed row limit or chunk-size setting. Store traversal is not globally key-sorted, and clusters need not have adjacent allocations. Sparse clusters add allocations and store metadata, and ordinary queries and kernels pay binding and traversal costs once per physical store. Staging In partition mode, creation and component transitions place rows in a staging store until maintenance. Queries and kernels visit staged rows. Same-composition replacement stays in its current store until refreshed. Maintenance releases empty cluster and staging allocations; nonempty stores keep their capacity. Destination growth can relocate existing rows. Dirty tracking Declared writable kernel ranges (host, threaded, and device copy-back), setters, and mutable storage.get mark affected classifier inputs, conservatively, even when only read. read and read-only queries do not. Writes to unrelated components never mark. Untracked writes Raw pointers and low-level storage writes bypass tracking. Call world.storage.mark_spatial_dirty(entity) per affected live entity, or World.invalidate_spatial for a full rebuild; external policy changes also need full invalidation. Both calls move no rows. Work per pass A clean pass touches no rows. Each dirty eligible entity is classified once per pass. Registration, structural changes, and full invalidation request a full rebuild; if every allocated entity is dirty, maintenance classifies contiguously. Active passes still copy identity-capacity keys and rebuild a temporary cluster directory. Failure All fallible classification and reorder planning precedes row movement. Classifier errors preserve committed keys, row order, and dirty state for a retry. Fatal allocation or lifecycle failures offer no rollback.
data.synchronization-primitives#Synchronizati:
These standalone primitives operate on storage you own. Larecs does not bind them to kernels: an AtomicView or SyncView, or an aggregate containing one, is rejected as an ordinary resource or capture. A custom mutable adapter may implement an atomic protocol over its own target-local buffers.
Topic Contract Atomic scalars UInt32 and Int32 only. Add and subtract wrap at that width and return the previous value. Strong compare_exchange returns success and the observed value. Read views permit loads only. Ordering Operations default to relaxed ordering, passed at compile time. Loads also accept acquire, stores release, and read-modify-write operations acquire, release, or acquire-release. Relaxed counters do not publish adjacent ordinary data. Guards use acquire and release internally. Guards Multiple read guards may coexist; a writer excludes all guards. try_read and try_write make at most one compare-exchange attempt. A false is_acquired means Busy, including a changed state or reader saturation; there is no wait, fairness, lock upgrade, or retry. Guard lifetime Owners and guards are noncopyable; copied views share one protection state. References from guard.value() stay within the guard’s lifetime. Scope exit, including error unwinding, or guard^.release() releases access. Errors do not roll back payload writes. CPU, NVIDIA, AMD The full scalar and guard operation set, with CPU-wide or whole-device scope. Apple device Relaxed or acquire loads, relaxed or release stores, and relaxed add and subtract. Strong compare-exchange, ordered add and subtract, and guards fail to compile. Device memory Payload and state must be aligned, initialized, device-accessible, and alive until completion. Unsafe view constructors do not allocate, transfer, or validate that memory. One canonical unlocked state must protect every overlapping guarded payload. Host and device allocations are separate domains; the primitives do not permit concurrent CPU and GPU access to one allocation.

data:
Build a particle simulation one feature at a time. Each stage is a complete program in examples/particles/.
Install Larecs: set up the locked environment and run the first program. Your first simulation: move particles with a system and a kernel, and check where they end up. Create and remove particles: create a batch of particles and remove the stationary one. Share time and configuration: set the step length from a configuration resource before each movement step. After the first program, Model data with entities and components explains how ECS identities and data fit the simulation.
The guides cover each topic in depth: entities and components, systems and kernels, batch creation and removal, and resources.

In this tutorial you build a program that moves particles across a plane and checks where they end up. You define the particle data, write the movement logic once, and let Larecs apply it to every particle that can move.
You need a working Mojo installation and the Larecs source, as described in Installation. The tutorial assumes you can read basic Mojo: structs, functions, and var declarations.
data.check-the-result#Check the result:
After ten steps of 0.1, walker has moved one unit along x and climber two units along y. marker has not moved:
ref storage = scheduler.world.storage assert_almost_equal(storage.get[Position](walker).x, 1.0) assert_almost_equal(storage.get[Position](climber).y, 2.0) assert_almost_equal(storage.get[Position](marker).x, -3.0) print("All particles reached their expected positions.") Read components back through scheduler.world.storage with the entity handles from add_entity. assert_almost_equal tolerates the rounding error of adding 0.1 ten times.
data.create-the-world#Create the world:
A World stores all entities, components, and resources. Its parameters list every component type the world can hold:
var world = World[Position, Velocity]() world.resources.add(Time(delta=0.1)) var walker = world.storage.add_entity(Position(0, 0), Velocity(1, 0)) var climber = world.storage.add_entity(Position(5, 0), Velocity(0, 2)) var marker = world.storage.add_entity(Position(-3, -3)) add_entity creates an entity with the given components and returns its Entity handle. walker and climber have both components. marker has only a position, so move never visits it.
data.describe-particles-with-components#Descr:
An entity is a particle’s identity: a handle with no data of its own. Components are the data you attach to an entity. A particle has a position and a velocity:
@fieldwise_init struct Position(Copyable, Movable): """Where a particle is.""" var x: Float64 """Horizontal coordinate.""" var y: Float64 """Vertical coordinate.""" @fieldwise_init struct Velocity(Copyable, Movable): """How far a particle moves per unit of time.""" var dx: Float64 """Horizontal speed.""" var dy: Float64 """Vertical speed.""" Components are ordinary structs. @fieldwise_init generates the constructor Position(x, y), and Copyable and Movable let Larecs store and move the values. Each component type appears at most once per entity.
data.next-steps#Next steps:
Continue with Create and remove particles, then Share time and configuration.
SystemContext.run lists every way to run a kernel, including the errors it raises. Inspect entities outside a kernel shows how to read entities with a query. Share values with resources covers adding, reading, and changing resources.
data.run-the-scheduler#Run the scheduler:
The Scheduler owns the world and calls your systems in the order you add them:
var scheduler = Scheduler[Position, Velocity](world^) scheduler.add_system(Move()) scheduler.run(steps=10) Scheduler[Position, Velocity] repeats the world’s component types because the scheduler’s type must match the world it owns. world^ transfers ownership of the world to the scheduler; world is no longer usable afterwards. run(steps=10) initializes every system, calls each update ten times, and finalizes every system.
data.share-the-step-length-as-a-resource#Shar:
Every particle moves for the same amount of simulated time per step. Data that exists once for the whole simulation, rather than once per particle, is a resource:
@fieldwise_init struct Time(Copyable, Movable): """The simulated time that passes in one step.""" var delta: Float64 """Step length."""
data.the-program#The program:
The complete program is a single file. You can open it now, or read it piece by piece below.
Complete program: examples/particles/movement.mojo """Moves particles with constant velocities for a fixed number of steps. This is the complete program of the "Your first simulation" tutorial. """ from std.testing import assert_almost_equal from larecs import ( Filter, KernelContext, Resources, Scheduler, System, SystemContext, World, ) @fieldwise_init struct Position(Copyable, Movable): """Where a particle is.""" var x: Float64 """Horizontal coordinate.""" var y: Float64 """Vertical coordinate.""" @fieldwise_init struct Velocity(Copyable, Movable): """How far a particle moves per unit of time.""" var dx: Float64 """Horizontal speed.""" var dy: Float64 """Vertical speed.""" @fieldwise_init struct Time(Copyable, Movable): """The simulated time that passes in one step.""" var delta: Float64 """Step length.""" comptime move_filter = Filter().include[Position]().read[Velocity]() comptime move_resources = Resources().read[Time]() def move(context: KernelContext[move_filter, move_resources]): """Advances every particle by its velocity times the step length. Args: context: The matching rows and the declared resources. """ ref time = context.resources.get[Time]() for particle in context: ref position = particle.get[Position]() ref velocity = particle.get[Velocity]() position.x += velocity.dx * time.delta position.y += velocity.dy * time.delta @fieldwise_init struct Move(System): """Runs the `move` kernel once per step.""" def update(mut self, mut context: SystemContext[...]) raises: """Moves all particles. Args: context: Access to the scheduler's world. Raises: Error: If `Time` is missing from the world. """ context.run[move]() def main() raises: """Runs the simulation and checks the final positions. Raises: Error: If the simulation fails or a position differs from the expected value. """ var world = World[Position, Velocity]() world.resources.add(Time(delta=0.1)) var walker = world.storage.add_entity(Position(0, 0), Velocity(1, 0)) var climber = world.storage.add_entity(Position(5, 0), Velocity(0, 2)) var marker = world.storage.add_entity(Position(-3, -3)) var scheduler = Scheduler[Position, Velocity](world^) scheduler.add_system(Move()) scheduler.run(steps=10) ref storage = scheduler.world.storage assert_almost_equal(storage.get[Position](walker).x, 1.0) assert_almost_equal(storage.get[Position](climber).y, 2.0) assert_almost_equal(storage.get[Position](marker).x, -3.0) print("All particles reached their expected positions.") View the source on GitHub
Run it from the repository root:
pixi run mojo run -I src examples/particles/movement.mojo It prints All particles reached their expected positions.
data.what-happened-in-each-step#What happened:
Scroll horizontally to read the full figure.
One context.run[move]() call. Larecs keeps entities with the same set of components together in one store. The filter decides which stores move sees: the store with Position and Velocity gets a KernelContext, and move visits its rows in order. The store without Velocity is skipped entirely.
On the host, context.run[move]() calls move once for each non-empty store that matches the filter, one after the other, and returns when all calls have finished. Write kernels so that each call handles only the rows of its own context; a world with more component combinations has more stores and therefore more calls per step.
data.write-the-movement-kernel#Write the move:
A kernel is a function that Larecs calls with a KernelContext. Iterating the context visits every particle that matches the kernel’s filter:
comptime move_filter = Filter().include[Position]().read[Velocity]() comptime move_resources = Resources().read[Time]() def move(context: KernelContext[move_filter, move_resources]): """Advances every particle by its velocity times the step length. Args: context: The matching rows and the declared resources. """ ref time = context.resources.get[Time]() for particle in context: ref position = particle.get[Position]() ref velocity = particle.get[Velocity]() position.x += velocity.dx * time.delta position.y += velocity.dy * time.delta move_filter declares two things at compile time:
Which particles match. Only entities with both Position and Velocity are visited. How the kernel accesses each component. include[Position]() grants read-write access, and read[Velocity]() grants read-only access. Larecs rejects writes to Velocity at compile time. move_resources declares that the kernel reads Time. A kernel can access only the resources it declares.
The trailing () after each step of the filter turns the description into a value. ref binds a reference to the stored component, so assigning to position.x changes the particle in place.

data:
In this tutorial you extend the movement program with a system that creates three moving particles and removes the stationary marker. You learn how to change which entities exist without affecting the particles you did not create.
The program keeps Position, Velocity, Time, move, and Move from the first tutorial unchanged.
data.check-the-result#Check the result: ref storage = scheduler.world.storage assert_almost_equal(storage.get[Position](walker).x, 1.0) assert_almost_equal(storage.get[Position](climber).y, 2.0) assert_equal(len(storage.query[Filter().include[Position]()]()), 5) var spawned_count = 0 for row in storage.query[move_filter](): var entity = row.get_entity() if entity != walker and entity != climber: assert_almost_equal(row.get[Position]().x, 1.1) assert_almost_equal(row.get[Position]().y, 0.0) spawned_count += 1 assert_equal(spawned_count, 3) print("Created three particles and removed the stationary marker.") walker and climber end where they did in the first tutorial. Each new particle starts at x=0.1 and moves ten steps of 0.1, so it ends at x=1.1. The marker is gone, so five particles have a position.
data.create-the-batch-in-a-system#Create the:
Creating and removing entities changes the world’s structure. Do it inside a system, here in initialize, which runs once before the first step:
@fieldwise_init struct Spawn(System): """Creates and moves only the new particles at initialization.""" def initialize(mut self, mut context: SystemContext[...]) raises: """Creates a scoped batch. Args: context: Access to the simulation world. Raises: Error: If creation or movement fails. """ with context.add_entities(Position(9, 9), count=3) as selected: selected.add(Velocity(1, 0)) selected.run[reset_position]() selected.run[move]() context.world[].storage.remove_entities[ Filter().include[Position]().exclude[Velocity]() ]() def update(mut self, mut context: SystemContext[...]) raises: """Leaves creation to initialization. Args: context: Access to the simulation world. """ pass context.add_entities(Position(9, 9), count=3) creates three particles and returns an EntitySelection of exactly those three. The with block binds that selection to selected:
selected.add(Velocity(1, 0)) gives the three particles a velocity. selected.run[reset_position]() moves them to (0, 0). selected.run[move]() advances them once by Time.delta, so they start at x=0.1. Each selected.run visits only the selected particles, even though walker also has a Position and a Velocity. While the block is open, the selection holds a structural lock: Larecs rejects any other entity creation, entity deletion, or component addition or removal in the world. The lock ends when the block ends, also on an error.
After the block, context.world[].storage.remove_entities deletes every entity that has a Position and no Velocity. In this world, that is marker. context.world is a pointer to the scheduler’s world; [] dereferences it. Spawn leaves update empty because it does all its work once.
data.inspect-the-world-before-it-starts#Inspe:
Before the scheduler takes the world, main reads it with queries:
var query = world.storage.query[ Filter().read[Position]().exclude[Velocity]() ]() var query_copy = query.copy() for row in query^: assert_almost_equal(row.get[Position]().x, -3.0) assert_equal(row.get_entity(), marker) for _ in query_copy^: pass assert_equal( len(world.storage.query[Filter().read[Position]().exclusive()]()), 1 ) The first query visits every entity with a Position and no Velocity; here that is only marker. Each row reads the components the filter names, and get_entity() returns the row’s entity handle. A query holds a structural lock while it lives. for row in query^ consumes the query with ^, so the loop ends it and its lock. query.copy() makes a second query with its own cursor and lock, which the empty loop ends the same way. Every query must end before world^ moves the world into the scheduler. exclusive() matches only entities with exactly the listed components, so the count is 1. Inspect entities outside a kernel covers queries in detail.
data.next-steps#Next steps: Continue with Share time and configuration. Create and remove entities in batches covers selections, locks, and deletion in detail.
data.register-spawn-before-move#Register Spaw: var scheduler = Scheduler[Position, Velocity](world^) scheduler.add_system(Spawn()) scheduler.add_system(Move()) scheduler.run(steps=10) run initializes Spawn and Move in order, then updates them ten times. Move has no initialization, so the three new particles exist before the first movement step.
data.set-positions-without-reading-them#Set p:
New particles start at (9, 9). Before they move, a kernel resets them to the origin:
def reset_position(context: KernelContext[Filter().write[Position]()]): """Initializes every selected position without reading it. Args: context: Selected rows with write-only Position access. """ for particle in context: particle.set(Position(0, 0)) Filter().write[Position]() grants write-only access: the kernel can replace a position with set, but it cannot read one with get. A kernel that writes every value it touches needs no more than this.
data.the-program#The program:
Complete program: examples/particles/lifecycle.mojo """Creates a particle batch, moves it, and removes stationary particles. Region markers supply excerpts for the particle learning path. """ from std.testing import assert_almost_equal, assert_equal from larecs import ( Filter, KernelContext, Resources, Scheduler, System, SystemContext, World, ) @fieldwise_init struct Position(Copyable, Movable): """Where a particle is.""" var x: Float64 """Horizontal coordinate.""" var y: Float64 """Vertical coordinate.""" @fieldwise_init struct Velocity(Copyable, Movable): """How far a particle moves per unit of time.""" var dx: Float64 """Horizontal speed.""" var dy: Float64 """Vertical speed.""" @fieldwise_init struct Time(Copyable, Movable): """The simulated time that passes in one step.""" var delta: Float64 """Step length.""" comptime move_filter = Filter().include[Position]().read[Velocity]() comptime move_resources = Resources().read[Time]() def move(context: KernelContext[move_filter, move_resources]): """Advances every particle by its velocity times the step length. Args: context: The matching rows and the declared resources. """ ref time = context.resources.get[Time]() for particle in context: ref position = particle.get[Position]() ref velocity = particle.get[Velocity]() position.x += velocity.dx * time.delta position.y += velocity.dy * time.delta def reset_position(context: KernelContext[Filter().write[Position]()]): """Initializes every selected position without reading it. Args: context: Selected rows with write-only Position access. """ for particle in context: particle.set(Position(0, 0)) @fieldwise_init struct Spawn(System): """Creates and moves only the new particles at initialization.""" def initialize(mut self, mut context: SystemContext[...]) raises: """Creates a scoped batch. Args: context: Access to the simulation world. Raises: Error: If creation or movement fails. """ with context.add_entities(Position(9, 9), count=3) as selected: selected.add(Velocity(1, 0)) selected.run[reset_position]() selected.run[move]() context.world[].storage.remove_entities[ Filter().include[Position]().exclude[Velocity]() ]() def update(mut self, mut context: SystemContext[...]) raises: """Leaves creation to initialization. Args: context: Access to the simulation world. """ pass @fieldwise_init struct Move(System): """Runs the `move` kernel once per step.""" def update(mut self, mut context: SystemContext[...]) raises: """Moves all particles. Args: context: Access to the scheduler's world. Raises: Error: If `Time` is missing from the world. """ context.run[move]() def main() raises: """Runs the simulation and checks the final positions. Raises: Error: If the simulation fails or a position differs from the expected value. """ var world = World[Position, Velocity]() world.resources.add(Time(delta=0.1)) var walker = world.storage.add_entity(Position(0, 0), Velocity(1, 0)) var climber = world.storage.add_entity(Position(5, 0), Velocity(0, 2)) var marker = world.storage.add_entity(Position(-3, -3)) var query = world.storage.query[ Filter().read[Position]().exclude[Velocity]() ]() var query_copy = query.copy() for row in query^: assert_almost_equal(row.get[Position]().x, -3.0) assert_equal(row.get_entity(), marker) for _ in query_copy^: pass assert_equal( len(world.storage.query[Filter().read[Position]().exclusive()]()), 1 ) var scheduler = Scheduler[Position, Velocity](world^) scheduler.add_system(Spawn()) scheduler.add_system(Move()) scheduler.run(steps=10) ref storage = scheduler.world.storage assert_almost_equal(storage.get[Position](walker).x, 1.0) assert_almost_equal(storage.get[Position](climber).y, 2.0) assert_equal(len(storage.query[Filter().include[Position]()]()), 5) var spawned_count = 0 for row in storage.query[move_filter](): var entity = row.get_entity() if entity != walker and entity != climber: assert_almost_equal(row.get[Position]().x, 1.1) assert_almost_equal(row.get[Position]().y, 0.0) spawned_count += 1 assert_equal(spawned_count, 3) print("Created three particles and removed the stationary marker.") data:
Install the repository’s locked Pixi environment and run the first particle program. Then use Larecs from your own Pixi project, either as source or as a precompiled package.
Larecs runs on Linux x86-64 and macOS on Apple Silicon. Larecs 1.0.0b1 is a beta, so its APIs can still change. Pixi installs these dependencies:
Mojo >=1.0.0,<1.1.0 MAX >=26.5.0,<27 mojo-tracy >=1.1.0,<2 It resolves them from the channels conda-forge, https://repo.prefix.dev/max, and https://prefix.dev/tree-d (for mojo-tracy). pixi.lock pins the exact builds.
data.install-the-locked-environment#Install t:
Install Pixi, then run:
git clone https://github.com/larecs/larecs.git cd larecs pixi install --locked pixi run mojo --version pixi run mojo run -I src examples/particles/movement.mojo The program prints All particles reached their expected positions. and fails with an assertion error if a particle ends elsewhere. It runs on the host and needs no accelerator. To reproduce a result later, keep the checkout revision together with its pixi.lock.
Continue with Your first simulation, which explains this program.
data.troubleshooting#Troubleshooting: Symptom Fix Import error for larecs Point -I at a directory that contains larecs/ source or larecs.mojoc. Compiler errors after a toolchain upgrade Restore the locked environment with pixi install --locked and rebuild the package. macOS linker error mentioning arm64e.x1 or libSystem.tbd Install an older macOS SDK. With SDKROOT unset, the repository’s activation script selects a compatible one; your own project needs the activation entry above. See the SDK workaround.
data.use-a-precompiled-package#Use a precompi:
Build the package with the toolchain your application uses. From the repository root:
mkdir -p /tmp/larecs-package pixi run mojo precompile src/larecs -o /tmp/larecs-package/larecs.mojoc pixi run mojo run -I /tmp/larecs-package examples/particles/movement.mojo Copy larecs.mojoc to your project’s include directory. Your application’s environment must provide compatible Mojo, MAX, and mojo-tracy builds from the channels above. Rebuild the package after you change the toolchain or the Larecs revision.
data.use-the-source-from-your-own-project#Use:
Create a Pixi project next to your clone, add the same dependencies, and pass the clone’s src directory as an include path. From the directory that contains larecs/:
pixi init my-simulation -c conda-forge -c https://repo.prefix.dev/max -c https://prefix.dev/tree-d cd my-simulation pixi add "mojo>=1.0.0,<1.1.0" "max>=26.5.0,<27" "mojo-tracy>=1.1.0,<2" cp ../larecs/examples/particles/movement.mojo main.mojo pixi run mojo run -I ../larecs/src main.mojo main.mojo starts as a copy of the first simulation and prints the same line; replace it with your own program. Your project resolves its own environment, so keep its version ranges in line with Larecs’s pixi.toml when you update the clone. For completion and diagnostics in your editor, add ../larecs/src to the Mojo language server’s include directories.
On macOS, the repository’s environment runs a script on activation that selects a macOS SDK the linker accepts; your project does not inherit it. Add it to your project’s pixi.toml:
[target.osx-arm64.activation] scripts = ["../larecs/scripts/activate_macos_sdk.sh"]

data: In this tutorial you extend the creation program so that a configuration value controls the step length. You add a second resource and a system that copies it into Time before every movement step.
data.add-a-configuration-resource-and-a-syste: @fieldwise_init struct Configuration(Copyable, Movable): """Shared configuration for subsequent movement steps.""" var delta: Float64 """Configured step length.""" @fieldwise_init struct ConfigureTime(System): """Sets the step length before movement.""" def update(mut self, mut context: SystemContext[...]) raises: """Reads configuration and updates shared time. Args: context: Access to the simulation resources. Raises: Error: If a required resource is missing. """ ref resources = context.world[].resources resources.get[Time]().delta = resources.get[Configuration]().delta Configuration is a resource like Time: one value for the whole world. ConfigureTime.update reads it through context.world[].resources and assigns its delta to Time.delta. ResourceStorage.get returns a reference, so the assignment changes the stored Time in place.
data.add-both-resources-to-the-world#Add both: var world = World[Position, Velocity]() world.resources.add(Time(delta=0.1), Configuration(delta=0.25)) var walker = world.storage.add_entity(Position(0, 0), Velocity(1, 0)) var climber = world.storage.add_entity(Position(5, 0), Velocity(0, 2)) _ = world.storage.add_entity(Position(-3, -3)) Time starts at 0.1 and Configuration holds 0.25. One ResourceStorage.add call adds both.
data.check-the-result#Check the result: ref storage = scheduler.world.storage assert_almost_equal(storage.get[Position](walker).x, 2.5) assert_almost_equal(storage.get[Position](climber).y, 5.0) assert_equal(len(storage.query[Filter().include[Position]()]()), 5) var spawned_count = 0 for row in storage.query[move_filter](): var entity = row.get_entity() if entity != walker and entity != climber: assert_almost_equal(row.get[Position]().x, 2.6) assert_almost_equal(row.get[Position]().y, 0.0) spawned_count += 1 assert_equal(spawned_count, 3) print("Configured time moved walker to x=2.5 and climber to y=5.") walker moves ten steps of 0.25 and ends at x=2.5; climber ends at y=5. The new particles start at x=0.1 and end at x=0.1 + 10 × 0.25 = 2.6.
data.next-steps#Next steps: Share values with resources covers resource permissions and what happens when a resource is missing. Update entities with systems and kernels covers filters, system order, and inspection.
data.order-the-systems#Order the systems:
var scheduler = Scheduler[Position, Velocity](world^) scheduler.add_system(Spawn()) scheduler.add_system(ConfigureTime()) scheduler.add_system(Move()) scheduler.run(steps=10) The Scheduler updates systems in the order you add them. ConfigureTime comes before Move, so every movement step uses 0.25. If you add ConfigureTime after Move, the first step still uses 0.1.
Spawn.initialize runs before any update. It moves the new particles once with the initial Time.delta of 0.1.
